**Scoping** (for [IAM Integration for Service Authentication](../mitigation-goals.md#iam-integration-for-service-authentication)): Your payment manager can authenticate callers of its data plane operations, such as `ProcessPayment`, by validating bearer tokens from an OpenID Connect identity provider. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore also supports IAM authorization for callers of these data plane operations.

**Configure via**

| Operation | Parameters |
|---|---|
| `bedrock-agentcore-control:CreatePaymentManager` | `$.authorizerType` |
| `bedrock-agentcore-control:UpdatePaymentManager` | `$.authorizerType` |

**Verify via**

| Operation | Parameters |
|---|---|

### Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.PaymentManager.4

An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payment manager's VPC Lattice resource gateway should have elastic network interfaces (ENIs) in more than one Availability Zone (AZ)

**Goal:** [Multi-AZ ENI Deployment](../mitigation-goals.md#multi-az-eni-deployment)

**Addresses:** [Threat.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.PaymentManager.5](#threatbedrock-agentcore-controlpaymentmanager5)

**Scoping** (for [Multi-AZ ENI Deployment](../mitigation-goals.md#multi-az-eni-deployment)): AgentCore creates your payment manager's VPC Lattice resource gateway with elastic network interfaces in the subnets you specify in `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds[*]`, the managed private endpoint's subnet list. Placing those network interfaces in more than one Availability Zone provides network-level redundancy and helps keep connectivity available when one zone is disrupted.

**Configure via**

| Operation | Parameters |

| `bedrock-agentcore-control:CreatePaymentManager` | `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds[*]` |
| `bedrock-agentcore-control:UpdatePaymentManager` | `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds[*]` |

|---|---|
| `bedrock-agentcore-control:GetPaymentManager` | `$.paymentManagerId` |

### Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.PaymentManager.5

An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payment manager that uses an inbound JWT authorizer to authenticate principals should be configured only with trusted OIDC identity providers

**Goal:** [Trusted SSO Configuration](../mitigation-goals.md#trusted-sso-configuration)

**Addresses:** [Threat.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.PaymentManager.3](#threatbedrock-agentcore-controlpaymentmanager3), [Threat.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.PaymentManager.6](#threatbedrock-agentcore-controlpaymentmanager6)

**Scoping** (for [Trusted SSO Configuration](../mitigation-goals.md#trusted-sso-configuration)): A payment manager with an inbound JWT authorizer authenticates callers of its data-plane operations through the OIDC identity provider whose discovery URL you set in the `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.discoveryUrl` request parameter. Configuring only trusted OIDC identity providers helps prevent an untrusted identity provider from being used to gain unintended access.

| `bedrock-agentcore-control:UpdatePaymentManager` | `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.allowedAudience[*]`, `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.allowedClients[*]`, `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.discoveryUrl`, `$.authorizerType` |

**Verify via**

| Operation | Parameters |
|---|---|

| `bedrock-agentcore-control:ListPaymentManagers` | *(any parameter)* |

### Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.PaymentManager.7

An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payment manager's managed VPC Lattice resource gateway should be associated only with security groups whose inbound and outbound rules restrict traffic to only the required sources, destinations, protocols, and ports

**Goal:** [Restrict Security Group Access](../mitigation-goals.md#restrict-security-group-access)

**Addresses:** [Threat.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.PaymentManager.10](#threatbedrock-agentcore-controlpaymentmanager10)

**Implemented by:** [Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.PaymentManager.15](#implementationbedrock-agentcore-controlpaymentmanager15), [Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.PaymentManager.16](#implementationbedrock-agentcore-controlpaymentmanager16)

**Scoping** (for [Restrict Security Group Access](../mitigation-goals.md#restrict-security-group-access)): When your payment manager's custom JWT authorizer uses a managed private endpoint, the security groups you specify in `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]`, or your VPC's default security group if you specify none, control traffic on the managed VPC Lattice resource gateway's network interfaces. Restricting the inbound and outbound rules to the required sources, destinations, protocols, and ports helps reduce the network exposure of your payment manager's managed VPC Lattice resource gateway.

**Configure via**

| `bedrock-agentcore-control:UpdatePaymentManager` | `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]` |

**Verify via**

| Operation | Parameters |
|---|---|
| `bedrock-agentcore-control:GetPaymentManager` | `$.paymentManagerId` |

### Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.PaymentManager.8

An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payment manager should be configured to send application and trace logs to CloudWatch Logs using vended logs delivery

**Goal:** [CloudWatch Logging - Vended Logs Delivery V2](../mitigation-goals.md#cloudwatch-logging---vended-logs-delivery-v2)

**Addresses:** [Threat.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.PaymentManager.8](#threatbedrock-agentcore-controlpaymentmanager8), [Threat.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.PaymentManager.9](#threatbedrock-agentcore-controlpaymentmanager9)

**Implemented by:** [Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.PaymentManager.17](#implementationbedrock-agentcore-controlpaymentmanager17), [Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.PaymentManager.18](#implementationbedrock-agentcore-controlpaymentmanager18)

**Scoping** (for [CloudWatch Logging - Vended Logs Delivery V2](../mitigation-goals.md#cloudwatch-logging---vended-logs-delivery-v2)): Amazon Bedrock AgentCore produces application logs and trace spans for every data plane API call against your payment manager, the span recording the payment manager, payment session, payment instrument and, for `ProcessPayment`, the amount and merchant. Sending those logs to CloudWatch Logs using vended logs delivery provides security-relevant visibility.

**Configure via**

| Operation | Parameters |
|---|---|
| `cloudwatch-logs:CreateDelivery` | `$.deliveryDestinationArn`, `$.deliverySourceName` |

| `cloudwatch-logs:PutDeliverySource` | `$.logType` |

**Verify via**

| Operation | Parameters |
|---|---|
| `cloudwatch-logs:GetDelivery` | `$.id` |
| `cloudwatch-logs:GetDeliveryDestination` | `$.name` |
| `cloudwatch-logs:GetDeliverySource` | `$.name` |

### Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.PolicyEngine.1

An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore policy engine should be encrypted with an AWS KMS customer managed key

**Goal:** [KMS Customer Managed Key Encryption](../mitigation-goals.md#kms-customer-managed-key-encryption)

**Addresses:** [Threat.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.PolicyEngine.1](#threatbedrock-agentcore-controlpolicyengine1), [Threat.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.PolicyEngine.3](#threatbedrock-agentcore-controlpolicyengine3), [Threat.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.PolicyEngine.4](#threatbedrock-agentcore-controlpolicyengine4), [Threat.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.PolicyEngine.5](#threatbedrock-agentcore-controlpolicyengine5)

**Scoping** (for [KMS Customer Managed Key Encryption](../mitigation-goals.md#kms-customer-managed-key-encryption)): A policy engine accepts a symmetric AWS KMS customer managed key in the `$.encryptionKeyArn` request parameter only when you create it. That key encrypts the engine and all of its policies and policy generations at rest for the engine's lifetime. Unlike the default AWS owned key, a customer managed key gives you control over its lifecycle and permissions and lets you audit its use.

| `bedrock-agentcore-control:ListPolicyEngineSummaries` | *(any parameter)* |
| `bedrock-agentcore-control:ListPolicyEngines` | *(any parameter)* |

### Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Registry.4

An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore registry's private endpoint should be associated only with security groups whose inbound and outbound rules restrict traffic to only the required sources, destinations, protocols, and ports

An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore registry record's sync role should be assumed only by AgentCore acting on behalf of trusted resources

**Goal:** [Restrict IAM Role Assumption - Service or Execution Role](../mitigation-goals.md#restrict-iam-role-assumption---service-or-execution-role)

**Addresses:** [Threat.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.RegistryRecord.1](#threatbedrock-agentcore-controlregistryrecord1)

**Verify via**

| Operation | Parameters |
|---|---|
| `bedrock-agentcore-control:GetRegistryRecord` | `$.recordId`, `$.registryId` |

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.1

*Resource policy — Preventive*

Attaches to `AWS::EC2::VPCEndpoint` and governs the IAM permissions below.

| Actions | Resources | Condition keys |
|---|---|---|
| `*` | `*` | `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` |
| `*` | `*` | `aws:ResourceOrgID` (alternatives: `aws:ResourceAccount`, `aws:ResourceOrgPaths`) |

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-control1)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-control1)): This implementation guidance recommends using your VPC endpoint policy to govern Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Control API calls made through the endpoint with the `aws:ResourceOrgID` condition key. As a result, calls to resources outside your organization are restricted, while AWS services acting on your behalf (`aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`) remain exempt.

**Reference:** To restrict access to trusted resources, use the `aws:ResourceOrgID`, `aws:ResourceOrgPaths`, or `aws:ResourceAccount` condition keys. These scope access to resources that belong to a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. Use `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` to allow AWS services to use their service principals to send requests from your network. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.
- [Establishing a resource perimeter](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies_data-perimeters.html#access_policies_data-perimeters-resource)

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.2

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.AgentRuntime.1

*Service control policy (SCP) — Preventive*

Governs the IAM permissions below.

| Actions | Resources | Condition keys |
|---|---|---|
| `*` | `*` | `aws:PrincipalTag/dp:exclude:network`, `aws:PrincipalTag/dp:include:network`, `aws:SourceIp`, `aws:SourceVpc` (alternatives: `aws:SourceVpce`), `aws:ViaAWSService` |
| `*` | `*` | `aws:RequestedRegion`, `aws:SourceVpc` |

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.AgentRuntime.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlagentruntime1)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.AgentRuntime.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlagentruntime1)): This implementation guidance recommends applying the `aws:PrincipalTag/dp:include:network`, `aws:SourceIp`, and `aws:SourceVpc` condition keys in a service control policy (SCP), pairing `aws:SourceVpc` with `aws:RequestedRegion`. These conditions help restrict requests made with your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime's execution role credentials to expected networks, while exempting AWS services that call through forward access sessions (`aws:ViaAWSService`). Apply the tag only to the execution role of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtimes whose `$.networkConfiguration.networkMode`, the runtime's network mode, is `VPC`, because in `PUBLIC` network mode an agent runtime's requests originate from an AWS-managed network, outside your expected networks.

**Data perimeter** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.AgentRuntime.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlagentruntime1)): The default network perimeter service control policy (SCP) samples apply their restriction to IAM principals tagged with `dp:include:network` set to `true`. Tag your AgentCore Runtime execution role with this tag so that the network perimeter applies to the calls it makes. If your execution role assumes another role as part of its operations, apply the same restriction to the assumed role.
- [Network perimeter SCP example using aws:SourceVpc](https://github.com/aws-samples/data-perimeter-policy-examples/blob/main/service_control_policies/network_perimeter_sourcevpc_scp.json)
- [Network perimeter SCP example using aws:VpceOrgID](https://github.com/aws-samples/data-perimeter-policy-examples/blob/main/service_control_policies/network_perimeter_vpceorgid_scp.json)
- [Network perimeter guidance for the data perimeter SCP examples](https://github.com/aws-samples/data-perimeter-policy-examples/blob/main/service_control_policies/README.md#sidenforcenetworkperimetervpceorgid)

**Reference:** To restrict access to expected networks at scale, use the `aws:VpceOrgID`, `aws:VpceOrgPaths`, or `aws:VpceAccount` condition keys where supported. These scope access to VPC endpoints owned by accounts within a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. These keys are preferred for enforcing network perimeter controls across multiple accounts because they do not require you to enumerate individual VPCs or endpoints. For finer-grained control, use the `aws:SourceVpc` or `aws:SourceVpce` condition keys to restrict access to a specific VPC or VPC endpoint. Use them also for services that do not currently support the `aws:VpceOrgID`, `aws:VpceOrgPaths`, or `aws:VpceAccount` condition keys. Because VPC IDs are unique only within a Region, pair `aws:SourceVpc` with `aws:RequestedRegion`. Use `aws:SourceIp` with your public IP ranges for requests that do not traverse a VPC endpoint. Use `aws:ViaAWSService` to exempt AWS services that call with your credentials through forward access sessions (FAS). Use `aws:PrincipalTag/tag-key` to apply the restriction to principals whose credentials can be used outside your expected networks, tagged with the selected key and value. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.
- [Establishing a network perimeter](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies_data-perimeters.html#access_policies_data-perimeters-network)
- [SCP sample: network perimeter policy with aws:VpceOrgID](https://github.com/aws-samples/data-perimeter-policy-examples/blob/main/service_control_policies/network_perimeter_vpceorgid_scp.json)

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.AgentRuntime.2

*CloudFormation hook — Proactive*

Validates template properties before provisioning.

- `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Runtime`: `$.RoleArn`

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.AgentRuntime.2](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlagentruntime2)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.AgentRuntime.2](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlagentruntime2)): This implementation guidance recommends validating the trust policy of `$.RoleArn`, your agent runtime's execution role, including source conditions on service principals, before provisioning. This helps prevent the agent runtime from being provisioned when that trust policy can grant public access, or role assumption beyond the reference policy you maintain.

**Reference:** This implementation recommends using IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks. Custom policy checks (`CheckNoPublicAccess`, `CheckNoNewAccess`) use automated reasoning to provide a higher level of assurance. They provably verify that a policy does not grant public access or grant new access beyond a reference policy you maintain. The first reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` allowlists the principals this role's trust policy may grant assumption to. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption beyond that allowlist. Example reference policies for role trust policies are available in the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples repository. The second reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` encodes the source conditions you accept when the service principal assumes the role: one statement per accepted combination of the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, with placeholders for your account, organization, and resource values. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption that no statement of the reference allows, including grants that omit the condition keys or weaken them with `IfExists`.
- [IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access-analyzer-custom-policy-checks.html)
- [IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples](https://github.com/aws-samples/iam-access-analyzer-custom-policy-check-samples)

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.AgentRuntime.3

*AWS Config rule — Detective*

A periodic rule that evaluates via the API operation chain below.

1. Call `bedrock-agentcore-control:ListAgentRuntimes`; check `$.agentRuntimes[*].agentRuntimeId`
2. Call `bedrock-agentcore-control:ListAgentRuntimeVersions` with `$.agentRuntimeId`; check `$.agentRuntimes[*].agentRuntimeVersion`
3. Call `bedrock-agentcore-control:GetAgentRuntime` with `$.agentRuntimeId`, `$.agentRuntimeVersion`; check `$.roleArn`
4. Call `iam:GetRole` with `$.RoleName`; check `$.Role.AssumeRolePolicyDocument`
5. Call `accessanalyzer:CheckNoPublicAccess` with `$.policyDocument`, `$.resourceType` = `AWS::IAM::AssumeRolePolicyDocument`; check `$.result`
6. Call `accessanalyzer:CheckNoNewAccess` with `$.newPolicyDocument`, `$.existingPolicyDocument`, `$.policyType` = `RESOURCE_POLICY`; check `$.result`
7. Call `accessanalyzer:CheckNoNewAccess` with `$.newPolicyDocument`, `$.existingPolicyDocument`, `$.policyType` = `RESOURCE_POLICY`; check `$.result`

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.AgentRuntime.2](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlagentruntime2)

Flagging trust policies that allow public role assumption, or assumption beyond your reference policy, or that omit the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, helps you detect overly permissive role assumption.

**Reference:** This implementation recommends using IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks.

Custom policy checks (`CheckNoPublicAccess`, `CheckNoNewAccess`) use automated reasoning to provide a higher level of assurance. They provably verify that a policy does not grant public access or grant new access beyond a reference policy you maintain.

The first reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` allowlists the principals this role's trust policy may grant assumption to. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption beyond that allowlist. Example reference policies for role trust policies are available in the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples repository.

The second reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` encodes the source conditions you accept when the service principal assumes the role: one role-assumption statement per accepted combination of the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, with placeholders for your account, organization, and resource values. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption that no statement of the reference allows, including grants that omit the condition keys or weaken them with `IfExists`.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.AgentRuntime.13

*Guidance — Directive*

When you connect an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime to your VPC (network mode `VPC`), supply two or more subnets in different Availability Zones. Set them in `$.networkConfiguration.networkModeConfig.subnets[*]` when you call `CreateAgentRuntime` or `UpdateAgentRuntime`, or in the `NetworkConfiguration` property of `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Runtime` in AWS CloudFormation. AgentCore creates elastic network interfaces (ENIs) for the runtime in the subnets you specify. Subnets in different zones place those ENIs in more than one Availability Zone. This helps the runtime's network connectivity survive the loss of a single zone. For runtimes on the Instances compute type, the capacity provider supplies the networking. Apply the same multi-AZ subnet selection to the subnets in the capacity provider's VPC configuration.

Availability Zone membership is a property of each subnet, not of the agent runtime. Before you supply subnet IDs, call the Amazon EC2 `DescribeSubnets` operation. Confirm from the `AvailabilityZone` and `AvailabilityZoneId` response fields that the subnets resolve to distinct Availability Zones. Also confirm that each zone ID is one that AgentCore supports for VPC connectivity in your Region. Subnets in unsupported zones cause the configuration to fail during resource creation. Standardize on infrastructure-as-code review so that the templates and modules that create agent runtimes consistently supply at least two subnets from different Availability Zones.

To verify the deployed state, call `GetAgentRuntime` and read `$.networkConfiguration.networkModeConfig.subnets[*]` from the response. Then resolve the Availability Zones of those subnets with `DescribeSubnets`. You can also enumerate the ENIs with `DescribeNetworkInterfaces`, filtered by those subnets and the runtime's security groups. If your account hides Amazon EC2 managed resources, set `IncludeManagedResources` to `true` so that the results include ENIs that AWS services manage. Confirm that those ENIs are in more than one Availability Zone. AgentCore shares these ENIs among runtimes that use the same subnet and security group configuration. A network settings change creates a new runtime version, and only the `DEFAULT` endpoint moves to it automatically. Call `UpdateAgentRuntimeEndpoint` for custom endpoints that pin earlier versions so that requests to them resolve to the multi-AZ configuration.

If your runtime mounts Amazon EFS or Amazon S3 Files access points, create a mount target in every Availability Zone that your runtime subnets use. An agent placed in a zone without a mount target can fail to mount the file system.

To assess and track multi-AZ posture at scale, you can use AWS Resilience Hub. Add the resources of the application that uses your agent runtime to a Resilience Hub application, and run a resiliency assessment. The assessment can flag single-AZ concentration against your resiliency policy. Before you rely on it for your agent runtime, confirm that Resilience Hub supports the runtime's resource type.

- [Subnets for your VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/configure-subnets.html)
- [DescribeSubnets (Amazon EC2 API Reference)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/APIReference/API_DescribeSubnets.html)
- [What is AWS Resilience Hub?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/resilience-hub/latest/userguide/what-is.html)

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.AgentRuntime.6](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlagentruntime6)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.AgentRuntime.6](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlagentruntime6)): This implementation guidance recommends supplying two or more subnets from different Availability Zones in `$.networkConfiguration.networkModeConfig.subnets[*]`, the subnets in your agent runtime's VPC network configuration. Spreading the elastic network interfaces that Amazon Bedrock AgentCore creates for your agent runtime across zones helps the runtime's VPC connectivity survive the loss of a single Availability Zone.

As a result, principals outside the accounts you name are restricted from invoking your runtime and its sessions, even when they know its ARN. Compare the full recorded URL, host and path, with the discovery URLs you trust. A provider such as Amazon Cognito serves every user pool from one regional host (`cognito-idp.<region>.amazonaws.com`). It identifies each pool only by the user pool ID segment of the path. If necessary, remediate with the responsive controls of your choice.

*Resource policy — Preventive*

| Actions | Resources | Condition keys |
|---|---|---|
| `bedrock-agentcore:*` | `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:runtime/${RuntimeId}` | `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`, `aws:PrincipalOrgID` (alternatives: `aws:PrincipalAccount`, `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`) |
| `bedrock-agentcore:*` | `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:runtime/${RuntimeId}` | `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID` (alternatives: `aws:SourceOrgPaths`) |

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.AgentRuntime.9](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlagentruntime9)): This implementation guidance recommends governing Amazon Bedrock AgentCore API calls against your agent runtime with the `aws:PrincipalOrgID` condition key in its resource-based policy, while exempting AWS services that access it on your behalf (`aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`) and scoping those service requests with `aws:SourceOrgID`. These conditions help prevent identities outside your organization from accessing your agent runtime.

**Reference:** Confirm that resource-based policies grant access only to trusted identities and to services acting on your behalf. As a defense-in-depth measure, use the `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`, or `aws:PrincipalAccount` condition keys to restrict access to trusted identities. These scope access to IAM principals within a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. These keys do not contain your organization or account values for requests by AWS service principals, so apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `false`. To restrict service access to your resources, use the `aws:SourceOrgID`, `aws:SourceOrgPaths`, `aws:SourceAccount`, or `aws:SourceArn` condition keys. These scope access performed on behalf of resources within a particular organization, specific organizational units, a specific AWS account, or a particular resource, respectively. Apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `true`. Also require that `aws:SourceAccount` is present in the request context, because not every service integration populates these keys. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.
- [Establishing an identity perimeter](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies_data-perimeters.html#access_policies_data-perimeters-identity)

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.AgentRuntime.22

*CloudFormation hook — Proactive*

Validates template properties before provisioning.

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.AgentRuntime.9](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlagentruntime9)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.AgentRuntime.9](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlagentruntime9)): This implementation guidance recommends validating `$.Policy`, the resource-based policy document for your agent runtime, before provisioning the resource-based policy on that runtime. The hook helps prevent a policy that can grant access beyond your reference policy, permissions you specify, or access to an AWS service principal beyond a reference policy containing the source conditions you accept from being provisioned.

**Reference:** This implementation recommends using IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks. Custom policy checks (`CheckNoNewAccess`, `CheckAccessNotGranted`) use automated reasoning to provide a higher level of assurance. They provably verify that a policy does not grant new access beyond a reference policy you maintain or grant specified permissions. The first reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` allowlists the principals that may be granted access to the resource. The check fails when the resource-based policy grants access beyond that allowlist. Example reference policies for resource-based policies are available in the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples repository. The second reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` encodes the source conditions you accept on grants to an AWS service principal: one statement per accepted combination of the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, with placeholders for your account, organization, and resource values. The check fails when the policy grants a service principal access that no statement of the reference allows, including grants that omit the condition keys or weaken them with `IfExists`.
- [IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access-analyzer-custom-policy-checks.html)
- [IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples](https://github.com/aws-samples/iam-access-analyzer-custom-policy-check-samples)

4. Call `accessanalyzer:CheckAccessNotGranted` with `$.policyDocument`, `$.policyType` = `RESOURCE_POLICY`, `$.access[*].actions[*]`; check `$.result`

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.AgentRuntime.29

*Guidance — Directive*

Configure the security groups associated with your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent runtime following least-privilege best practices. In VPC network mode, the security groups in `$.networkConfiguration.networkModeConfig.securityGroups[*]` are attached to the elastic network interfaces (ENIs) that AgentCore creates in your subnets. These security groups control which resources your agent code can communicate with. Your runtime's custom JWT authorizer may reach a private identity provider through a managed VPC Lattice resource gateway. In that case, the security groups in `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]` govern that gateway's traffic. Specify those security groups explicitly, because the VPC's default security group is used when none are given.

Restrict both inbound and outbound rules on these security groups to only the required sources and destinations, protocols, and ports. Sources and destinations can be IP address ranges, referenced security groups, or prefix lists. Avoid rules that permit unrestricted access from or to any IP address (0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0), particularly on administrative or sensitive ports. Where the peer is an AWS resource in a security group, reference that security group instead of its address range. For example, reference the security group of a database or file system mount target that your agent code connects to. The rule then follows the peer's network interfaces rather than addresses that can change.

To govern security groups at scale, use AWS Firewall Manager security group policies across your organization in AWS Organizations. You can scope each policy by account, organizational unit (OU), or tag. A common security group policy applies a baseline security group. A content audit security group policy audits inbound and outbound rules against an allow list or block list. It flags noncompliant security groups in a central dashboard, sends notifications, and can automatically remediate noncompliant rules. Review the policy's findings before you enable automatic remediation. A usage audit security group policy can remove unused or redundant security groups.

To verify unintended access that your security groups permit, use Amazon VPC Network Access Analyzer. Define a Network Access Scope for the access you consider unintended. For example, the scope can match any path that reaches administrative ports 22 or 3389 from an unrestricted address. Create the scope by calling `CreateNetworkInsightsAccessScope`, run an analysis by calling `StartNetworkInsightsAccessScopeAnalysis`, and then review the findings. Network Access Analyzer reasons about the security group together with the route table, network ACL, and public IP assignment. This helps you identify unintended network access relative to your security and compliance requirements.

- [Using content audit security group policies with Firewall Manager](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/security-group-policies-audit.html)
- [How to continuously audit and limit security groups with AWS Firewall Manager](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/how-to-continuously-audit-and-limit-security-groups-with-aws-firewall-manager/)
- [What is Network Access Analyzer?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/network-access-analyzer/what-is-network-access-analyzer.html)

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.AgentRuntime.12](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlagentruntime12)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.AgentRuntime.12](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlagentruntime12)): This implementation guidance recommends restricting the inbound and outbound rules on your agent runtime's security groups to the required addresses, protocols, and ports. Excluding unrestricted addresses such as 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 from those inbound and outbound rules helps reduce the network exposure of your agent runtime.

|---|---|---|
| `bedrock-agentcore:*` | `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:runtime/${RuntimeId}/runtime-endpoint/${Name}` | `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`, `aws:PrincipalTag/dp:exclude:network`, `aws:SourceIp`, `aws:SourceVpc` (alternatives: `aws:SourceVpce`), `aws:ViaAWSService` |
| `bedrock-agentcore:*` | `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:runtime/${RuntimeId}/runtime-endpoint/${Name}` | `aws:RequestedRegion`, `aws:SourceVpc` |

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.AgentRuntimeEndpoint.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlagentruntimeendpoint1)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.AgentRuntimeEndpoint.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlagentruntimeendpoint1)): This implementation guidance recommends governing Amazon Bedrock AgentCore API calls against your agent runtime endpoint with the `aws:SourceIp`, `aws:SourceVpc`, and `aws:RequestedRegion` condition keys in its resource-based policy. These conditions help restrict those calls to expected networks, while exempting AWS services acting on your behalf (`aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`, `aws:ViaAWSService`) and tagged principals (`aws:PrincipalTag/dp:exclude:network`).

**Reference:** To restrict access to expected networks, use the `aws:SourceVpc` or `aws:SourceVpce` condition keys. These scope access to a specific VPC or VPC endpoint. Because VPC IDs are unique only within a Region, pair `aws:SourceVpc` with `aws:RequestedRegion`. Use `aws:SourceIp` with your public IP ranges for requests that do not traverse a VPC endpoint. Use `aws:ViaAWSService` to exempt AWS services that call with your credentials through forward access sessions (FAS). Use `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` to exempt AWS services that access your resources with their service principals. Use `aws:PrincipalTag/tag-key` to exempt principals that must legitimately operate from outside your expected networks. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.
- [Establishing a network perimeter](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies_data-perimeters.html#access_policies_data-perimeters-network)

The hook helps prevent a policy that can grant access beyond your reference policy, permissions you specify such as `bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntimeCommand`, or access to an AWS service principal beyond a reference policy containing the source conditions you accept from being provisioned.

**Reference:** This implementation recommends using IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks. Custom policy checks (`CheckNoNewAccess`, `CheckAccessNotGranted`) use automated reasoning to provide a higher level of assurance. They provably verify that a policy does not grant new access beyond a reference policy you maintain or grant specified permissions. The first reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` allowlists the principals that may be granted access to the resource. The check fails when the resource-based policy grants access beyond that allowlist. Example reference policies for resource-based policies are available in the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples repository. The second reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` encodes the source conditions you accept on grants to an AWS service principal: one statement per accepted combination of the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, with placeholders for your account, organization, and resource values. The check fails when the policy grants a service principal access that no statement of the reference allows, including grants that omit the condition keys or weaken them with `IfExists`.

Also use `aws:TagKeys` on the untag action so that a request removing either key is denied.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Browser.1

*Service control policy (SCP) — Preventive*

Governs the IAM permissions below.

| Actions | Resources | Condition keys |
|---|---|---|
| `*` | `*` | `aws:PrincipalTag/dp:exclude:network`, `aws:PrincipalTag/dp:include:network`, `aws:SourceIp`, `aws:SourceVpc` (alternatives: `aws:SourceVpce`), `aws:ViaAWSService` |
| `*` | `*` | `aws:RequestedRegion`, `aws:SourceVpc` |

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Browser.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlbrowser1)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Browser.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlbrowser1)): This implementation guidance recommends applying the `aws:PrincipalTag/dp:include:network`, `aws:SourceIp`, and `aws:SourceVpc` condition keys in a service control policy (SCP), pairing `aws:SourceVpc` with `aws:RequestedRegion`. These conditions help restrict requests made with your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore browser's execution role credentials to expected networks, while exempting AWS services that call through forward access sessions (`aws:ViaAWSService`). Apply the tag only to the execution role of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore browsers whose `$.networkConfiguration.networkMode`, the network mode setting, is `VPC`, because in `PUBLIC` network mode a browser's requests originate from an AWS-managed network, outside your expected networks.

**Data perimeter** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Browser.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlbrowser1)): The default network perimeter service control policy (SCP) samples apply only to IAM principals that carry the `dp:include:network` tag set to `true`. Apply this tag to your browser's execution role to help restrict requests made with its credentials to expected networks. If the execution role assumes another role, consider tagging the assumed role as well.
- [SCP sample: network perimeter policy with aws:SourceVpc](https://github.com/aws-samples/data-perimeter-policy-examples/blob/main/service_control_policies/network_perimeter_sourcevpc_scp.json)
- [SCP sample: network perimeter policy with aws:VpceOrgID](https://github.com/aws-samples/data-perimeter-policy-examples/blob/main/service_control_policies/network_perimeter_vpceorgid_scp.json)
- [Network perimeter guidance for the SCP examples](https://github.com/aws-samples/data-perimeter-policy-examples/blob/main/service_control_policies/README.md#sidenforcenetworkperimetervpceorgid)

**Reference:** To restrict access to expected networks at scale, use the `aws:VpceOrgID`, `aws:VpceOrgPaths`, or `aws:VpceAccount` condition keys where supported. These scope access to VPC endpoints owned by accounts within a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. These keys are preferred for enforcing network perimeter controls across multiple accounts because they do not require you to enumerate individual VPCs or endpoints. For finer-grained control, use the `aws:SourceVpc` or `aws:SourceVpce` condition keys to restrict access to a specific VPC or VPC endpoint. Use them also for services that do not currently support the `aws:VpceOrgID`, `aws:VpceOrgPaths`, or `aws:VpceAccount` condition keys. Because VPC IDs are unique only within a Region, pair `aws:SourceVpc` with `aws:RequestedRegion`. Use `aws:SourceIp` with your public IP ranges for requests that do not traverse a VPC endpoint. Use `aws:ViaAWSService` to exempt AWS services that call with your credentials through forward access sessions (FAS). Use `aws:PrincipalTag/tag-key` to apply the restriction to principals whose credentials can be used outside your expected networks, tagged with the selected key and value. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.
- [Establishing a network perimeter](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies_data-perimeters.html#access_policies_data-perimeters-network)
- [SCP sample: network perimeter policy with aws:VpceOrgID](https://github.com/aws-samples/data-perimeter-policy-examples/blob/main/service_control_policies/network_perimeter_vpceorgid_scp.json)

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Browser.2

*CloudFormation hook — Proactive*

Validates template properties before provisioning.

- `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::BrowserCustom`: `$.ExecutionRoleArn`

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Browser.2](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlbrowser2)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Browser.2](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlbrowser2)): This implementation guidance recommends validating the trust policy of `$.ExecutionRoleArn`, your browser's execution role, including source conditions on service principals, before provisioning. This helps prevent the browser from being provisioned when that trust policy can grant public access, or role assumption beyond the reference policy you maintain.

**Reference:** This implementation recommends using IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks. Custom policy checks (`CheckNoPublicAccess`, `CheckNoNewAccess`) use automated reasoning to provide a higher level of assurance. They provably verify that a policy does not grant public access or grant new access beyond a reference policy you maintain. The first reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` allowlists the principals this role's trust policy may grant assumption to. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption beyond that allowlist. Example reference policies for role trust policies are available in the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples repository. The second reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` encodes the source conditions you accept when the service principal assumes the role: one role-assumption statement per accepted combination of the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, with placeholders for your account, organization, and resource values. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption that no statement of the reference allows, including grants that omit the condition keys or weaken them with `IfExists`.
- [IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access-analyzer-custom-policy-checks.html)
- [IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples](https://github.com/aws-samples/iam-access-analyzer-custom-policy-check-samples)

**Reference:** This implementation recommends using IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks. The first reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` allowlists the principals this role's trust policy may grant assumption to. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption beyond that allowlist. Example reference policies for role trust policies are available in the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples repository. The second reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` encodes the source conditions you accept when the service principal assumes the role: one role-assumption statement per accepted combination of the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, with placeholders for your account, organization, and resource values. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption that no statement of the reference allows, including grants that omit the condition keys or weaken them with `IfExists`.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Browser.10

*Guidance — Directive*

This guidance applies to custom browsers that you create in the `VPC` network mode. When you call `CreateBrowser`, configure `networkConfiguration.vpcConfig.subnets` with two or more private subnets in different Availability Zones. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore creates elastic network interfaces (ENIs) for the browser in the subnets you specify. The Availability Zones of those subnets determine where the browser's ENIs exist. Spreading the ENIs across zones helps the browser keep network connectivity if a single Availability Zone becomes unavailable. Because a browser has no update operation, its subnet list is fixed at creation. To change the subnets, delete the browser and create it again.

Subnet-to-AZ membership is a property of each subnet, not of the browser. Before you supply subnet IDs, call the Amazon EC2 `DescribeSubnets` operation and confirm that the `AvailabilityZone` values differ. Also confirm that each subnet's `AvailabilityZoneId` is a zone that AgentCore supports for VPC connectivity in your Region. Subnets in unsupported zones cause browser creation to fail. Standardize on infrastructure-as-code review for the templates and modules that create your browsers. Confirm that each one supplies at least two subnets from different Availability Zones, for example in the `Subnets` property of `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::BrowserCustom`.

To verify the deployed state, call `GetBrowser` and read the subnet IDs returned in `networkConfiguration.vpcConfig.subnets`. Then call `DescribeNetworkInterfaces` with a `subnet-id` filter for those subnets. AgentCore tags the ENIs it manages with the `AmazonBedrockAgentCoreManaged` tag. Confirm that the returned ENIs span more than one Availability Zone. These ENIs can be shared with other AgentCore resources that use the same subnet and security group configuration.

To assess and track multi-AZ posture at scale, include the application resources around your browsers in an AWS Resilience Hub application. Then run a resiliency assessment against your resiliency policy. The assessment can flag resources concentrated in a single Availability Zone. The AWS Resilience Hub list of supported resources does not name Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Confirm which of your resources the assessment covers before you rely on it for your browsers.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Browser.16

*Guidance — Directive*

For an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore custom browser in VPC network mode, configure the security groups in `$.networkConfiguration.vpcConfig.securityGroups[*]` of your `CreateBrowser` request following least-privilege best practices. AgentCore attaches these groups to the elastic network interfaces that it creates in your subnets. Their inbound and outbound rules control which resources your browser sessions can communicate with. The association is set when you create the browser. You maintain least privilege through the rules on the referenced security groups. Restrict both inbound and outbound rules to only the required sources and destinations (IP address ranges, referenced security groups, or prefix lists), protocols, and ports. Avoid rules that permit unrestricted access from or to any address (0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0), particularly on administrative or sensitive ports. If your browser sessions need internet access through a NAT gateway, limit those outbound rules to the protocols and ports that your browsing workload requires. Where the peer is an AWS resource in a security group, reference that security group instead of its address range. The rule then follows the peer's network interfaces rather than addresses that can change.

To govern security groups at scale, use AWS Firewall Manager security group policies across your organization in AWS Organizations. You can scope these policies by account, organizational unit (OU), or tag. A common security group policy applies a baseline security group. A content audit security group policy audits inbound and outbound rules against an allow list or a block list. It flags noncompliant security groups in a central dashboard, sends notifications, and can automatically remediate them. A usage audit security group policy removes unused or redundant security groups. A content audit policy can evaluate the groups your browser references, because they are customer-created security groups. Before you rely on a common security group policy for your browser, confirm that Firewall Manager supports the network interfaces that AgentCore manages.

To verify unintended access that your security groups permit, use Amazon VPC Network Access Analyzer. Define a Network Access Scope for the access that you consider unintended. For example, match any path that reaches your browser's network interfaces on administrative ports 22 or 3389 from an unrestricted address. Create the scope with `CreateNetworkInsightsAccessScope`, run an analysis with `StartNetworkInsightsAccessScopeAnalysis`, and review the findings. Network Access Analyzer evaluates the security group together with the route table, network ACL, and public IP assignment. This helps you identify unintended network access relative to your security and compliance requirements.

- [Using content audit security group policies with Firewall Manager](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/security-group-policies-audit.html)
- [How to continuously audit and limit security groups with AWS Firewall Manager](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/how-to-continuously-audit-and-limit-security-groups-with-aws-firewall-manager/)
- [What is Network Access Analyzer?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/network-access-analyzer/what-is-network-access-analyzer.html)

Excluding unrestricted addresses such as 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 from those inbound and outbound rules helps reduce the network exposure of your browser.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.CapacityProvider.1

*Service control policy (SCP) — Preventive*

Governs the IAM permissions below.

| Actions | Resources | Condition keys |
|---|---|---|
| `*` | `*` | `aws:PrincipalTag/dp:exclude:network`, `aws:SourceIp`, `aws:SourceVpc` (alternatives: `aws:SourceVpce`), `aws:ViaAWSService`, `ec2:SourceInstanceARN` (alternatives: `aws:PrincipalTag/dp:include:network`) |
| `*` | `*` | `aws:RequestedRegion`, `aws:SourceVpc` |

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.CapacityProvider.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlcapacityprovider1)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.CapacityProvider.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlcapacityprovider1)): This implementation guidance recommends applying the `ec2:SourceInstanceARN`, `aws:SourceIp`, and `aws:SourceVpc` condition keys in a service control policy (SCP), pairing `aws:SourceVpc` with `aws:RequestedRegion`. These conditions help restrict requests made with your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore capacity provider's default instance role or instance profile credentials to expected networks, while exempting AWS services that call through forward access sessions (`aws:ViaAWSService`).

**Reference:** To restrict access to expected networks at scale, use the `aws:VpceOrgID`, `aws:VpceOrgPaths`, or `aws:VpceAccount` condition keys where supported. These scope access to VPC endpoints owned by accounts within a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. These keys are preferred for enforcing network perimeter controls across multiple accounts because they do not require you to enumerate individual VPCs or endpoints. For finer-grained control, use the `aws:SourceVpc` or `aws:SourceVpce` condition keys to restrict access to a specific VPC or VPC endpoint. Use them also for services that do not currently support the `aws:VpceOrgID`, `aws:VpceOrgPaths`, or `aws:VpceAccount` condition keys. Because VPC IDs are unique only within a Region, pair `aws:SourceVpc` with `aws:RequestedRegion`. Use `aws:SourceIp` with your public IP ranges for requests that do not traverse a VPC endpoint. Use `aws:ViaAWSService` to exempt AWS services that call with your credentials through forward access sessions (FAS). Use `ec2:SourceInstanceARN` to apply the restriction to the role sessions whose credentials can be used outside your expected networks. Alternatively, you can use `aws:PrincipalTag/tag-key`, tagging the roles with the tag key and value your IAM policy management strategy uses. For credentials delivered to an Amazon EC2 instance, you can use `aws:Ec2InstanceSourceVpc` and `aws:Ec2InstanceSourcePrivateIPv4` to bind them to the instance they were issued to. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

*CloudFormation hook — Proactive*

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.CapacityProvider.2](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlcapacityprovider2)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.CapacityProvider.2](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlcapacityprovider2)): This implementation guidance recommends validating the trust policies of `$.PermissionsConfiguration.CapacityProviderOperatorRoleArn` and `$.ComputeConfiguration.Ec2Configuration.LaunchTemplateSource.LaunchParameters.InstanceProfileArn`, your capacity provider's infrastructure role and instance role, including source conditions on service principals, before provisioning. This helps prevent the capacity provider from being provisioned when any trust policy can grant public access, or role assumption beyond the reference policy you maintain.

**Reference:** This implementation recommends using IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks. Custom policy checks (`CheckNoPublicAccess`, `CheckNoNewAccess`) use automated reasoning to provide a higher level of assurance. They provably verify that a policy does not grant public access or grant new access beyond a reference policy you maintain. The first reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` allowlists the principals this role's trust policy may grant assumption to. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption beyond that allowlist. Example reference policies for role trust policies are available in the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples repository. The second reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` encodes the source conditions you accept when the service principal assumes the role: one role-assumption statement per accepted combination of the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, with placeholders for your account, organization, and resource values. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption that no statement of the reference allows, including grants that omit the condition keys or weaken them with `IfExists`.
- [IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access-analyzer-custom-policy-checks.html)
- [IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples](https://github.com/aws-samples/iam-access-analyzer-custom-policy-check-samples)

*AWS Config rule — Detective*

A periodic rule that evaluates via the API operation chain below.

1. Call `bedrock-agentcore-control:ListCapacityProviders`; check `$.capacityProviders[*].capacityProviderId`
2. Call `bedrock-agentcore-control:GetCapacityProvider` with `$.capacityProviderId`; check `$.permissionsConfiguration.capacityProviderOperatorRoleArn`, `$.computeConfiguration.ec2Configuration.launchTemplateSource.launchParameters.instanceProfileArn`
3. Call `iam:GetInstanceProfile` with `$.InstanceProfileName`; check `$.InstanceProfile.Roles[*].RoleName`
4. Call `iam:GetRole` with `$.RoleName`; check `$.Role.AssumeRolePolicyDocument`
5. Call `accessanalyzer:CheckNoPublicAccess` with `$.policyDocument`, `$.resourceType` = `AWS::IAM::AssumeRolePolicyDocument`; check `$.result`
6. Call `accessanalyzer:CheckNoNewAccess` with `$.newPolicyDocument`, `$.existingPolicyDocument`, `$.policyType` = `RESOURCE_POLICY`; check `$.result`
7. Call `accessanalyzer:CheckNoNewAccess` with `$.newPolicyDocument`, `$.existingPolicyDocument`, `$.policyType` = `RESOURCE_POLICY`; check `$.result`

Flagging trust policies that allow public role assumption, or assumption beyond your reference policy, or that omit the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys on the infrastructure role, helps you detect overly permissive role assumption.

The first reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` allowlists the principals this role's trust policy may grant assumption to. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption that no statement of the reference allows, including grants that omit the condition keys or weaken them with `IfExists`.

*Resource control policy (RCP) — Preventive*

Governs the IAM permissions below.

| Actions | Resources | Condition keys |

| `sts:AssumeRole` | `*` | `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`, `aws:PrincipalOrgID` (alternatives: `aws:PrincipalAccount`, `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`) |
| `sts:AssumeRole` | `*` | `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID` (alternatives: `aws:SourceOrgPaths`) |

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.CapacityProvider.2](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlcapacityprovider2)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.CapacityProvider.2](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlcapacityprovider2)): This implementation guidance recommends restricting `sts:AssumeRole` with the `aws:PrincipalOrgID` condition key in a resource control policy (RCP), while exempting AWS services acting on your behalf (`aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`) and scoping those service requests with `aws:SourceOrgID`. These conditions help prevent principals outside your organization from assuming your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore capacity provider's infrastructure and instance roles, `$.permissionsConfiguration.capacityProviderOperatorRoleArn` and `$.computeConfiguration.ec2Configuration.launchTemplateSource.launchParameters.instanceProfileArn`.

**Reference:** To restrict access to trusted identities, use the `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`, or `aws:PrincipalAccount` condition keys. These scope access to IAM principals within a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. These keys do not contain your organization or account values for requests by AWS service principals, so apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `false`. As a defense-in-depth measure, use the `aws:SourceOrgID`, `aws:SourceOrgPaths`, `aws:SourceAccount`, or `aws:SourceArn` condition keys to restrict service access to your roles. These scope access performed on behalf of resources within a particular organization, specific organizational units, a specific AWS account, or a particular resource, respectively. Apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `true`. Also require that `aws:SourceAccount` is present in the request context, because not every service integration populates these keys. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.CapacityProvider.16

*Guidance — Directive*

Create each Amazon Bedrock AgentCore capacity provider with two or more subnets that reside in different Availability Zones (AZs). Supply these subnets in the VPC configuration of your `CreateCapacityProvider` request, at `$.computeConfiguration.ec2Configuration.vpcConfiguration.subnets[*]`. AgentCore launches the capacity provider's Amazon EC2 managed instances and their elastic network interfaces (ENIs) in these subnets. Agent runtimes on the Instances compute type inherit this networking. With subnets in more than one zone, the ENIs for your agent sessions can exist in more than one Availability Zone. This helps network connectivity survive the loss of a single zone.

Plan the subnet list before you create the capacity provider. The service accepts a single subnet. You also can't change the subnet list later, because `UpdateCapacityProvider` changes only the description. In AWS CloudFormation, changing the subnets of an `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::CapacityProvider` resource requires replacement. To move a single-zone capacity provider to multiple zones, create a new one, for example through the console's duplicate flow. Then associate your agent runtimes with the new capacity provider. Deleting the original capacity provider stops and deletes its sessions and their persistent storage. Copy out any session data you need before you delete it.

Subnet-to-AZ membership is a property of each subnet, not of the capacity provider. Before you supply subnet IDs, call the Amazon EC2 `DescribeSubnets` operation. Confirm from each subnet's `AvailabilityZone` field that the IDs belong to distinct Availability Zones. Standardize on infrastructure-as-code review so that every template and module that creates a capacity provider supplies subnets from at least two Availability Zones.

To verify the deployed configuration, call `GetCapacityProvider`. Confirm that the subnets in the returned VPC configuration resolve to more than one Availability Zone. To inspect running sessions, call the Amazon EC2 `DescribeInstances` operation with managed resources included. Filter on the `bedrock-agentcore:capacity-provider-id` tag key. You can also call `DescribeNetworkInterfaces` with `IncludeManagedResources` set to `true`. Confirm that the subnets of the attached network interfaces span more than one Availability Zone. Depending on your managed resource visibility setting, EC2 list operations can hide these resources unless you include managed resources. Instances exist only while sessions run. Treat the configured subnet list as the primary check.

Some constraints remain zonal. Amazon EBS volumes attach only to instances in the same Availability Zone. A session that resumes with persistent volumes may therefore depend on the zone where those volumes were created. Capacity Reservations also reserve capacity in a specific Availability Zone. If you use the `capacity-reservations-only` preference, target reservations in more than one of your subnets' Availability Zones.

To assess and track multi-AZ posture at scale, include your application's resources in an AWS Resilience Hub application. Then run a resiliency assessment to flag single-AZ concentration against your resiliency policy. AWS Resilience Hub does not list Amazon Bedrock AgentCore among its supported services. It may therefore report the capacity provider as unsupported. Use the assessment to complement the configuration checks above, not to replace them.

- [Subnets for your VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/configure-subnets.html)
- [DescribeSubnets (Amazon EC2 API Reference)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/APIReference/API_DescribeSubnets.html)
- [What is AWS Resilience Hub?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/resilience-hub/latest/userguide/what-is.html)

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.CapacityProvider.7](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlcapacityprovider7)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.CapacityProvider.7](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlcapacityprovider7)): This implementation guidance recommends supplying two or more subnets from different Availability Zones in `$.computeConfiguration.ec2Configuration.vpcConfiguration.subnets[*]`, the subnet list of your capacity provider's VPC configuration. Spreading the network interfaces that AgentCore creates for the capacity provider's instances across zones helps your agent sessions' connectivity survive the loss of a single Availability Zone.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.CapacityProvider.24

*Guidance — Directive*

Configure the security groups that you specify for your capacity provider in `$.computeConfiguration.ec2Configuration.vpcConfiguration.securityGroups[*]` on `CreateCapacityProvider` by following least-privilege best practices. AgentCore associates these groups with the Amazon EC2 managed instances that it launches in your VPC. Agent runtimes that use the capacity provider inherit this networking. Restrict both inbound and outbound rules to only the required sources and destinations (IP address ranges, referenced security groups, or prefix lists), protocols, and ports. Do not permit unrestricted access from or to 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0, particularly on administrative ports such as port 22 (SSH). A new security group includes an outbound rule that allows all outbound traffic. Replace that rule with rules for the specific destinations your agents require, and do not open broad outbound access unless your agents need it. Where the peer is an AWS resource in a security group, such as a database or an interface VPC endpoint that your agents connect to, reference that security group instead of its address range. The rule then follows the peer's network interfaces rather than addresses that can change. After you create a capacity provider, you can't change which security groups it uses, because `UpdateCapacityProvider` changes only the description. To use different groups, create a new capacity provider, for example through the console's duplicate flow. You can still tighten the rules in the referenced groups at any time. Rule changes apply automatically to all resources associated with each group.

To govern security groups at scale, use AWS Firewall Manager security group policies across your organization in AWS Organizations, scoped by account, OU, or tag. A common security group policy applies a baseline group to in-scope resources. Because you can't directly modify instances that AgentCore manages, a common policy may not be able to change their security group associations. A content audit policy audits inbound and outbound rules against an allow list or block list. It flags noncompliant groups in a central dashboard, sends notifications, and can automatically remediate. Include the Amazon VPC security group resource type in its scope so that the groups your capacity provider references are evaluated directly. Review the findings before you enable automatic remediation. A usage audit policy removes unused or redundant groups, and it can treat a group as unused when no EC2 instance or network interface uses it. AgentCore launches instances when your runtimes are invoked, so your capacity provider's groups can have no attached network interfaces between sessions. Review usage audit findings before you enable automatic removal. Deleting a group that your capacity provider references may prevent AgentCore from launching new instances.

To verify unintended access that your security groups permit, use Amazon VPC Network Access Analyzer. Define a Network Access Scope for the access you consider unintended, such as any path that reaches port 22 on your capacity provider's instances from an unrestricted address. Then run an analysis (`CreateNetworkInsightsAccessScope`, `StartNetworkInsightsAccessScopeAnalysis`) and review the findings. Network Access Analyzer reasons about the security group together with the route table, network ACL, and public IP assignment. It identifies unintended network access relative to your security and compliance requirements. Run analyses while your capacity provider has active sessions, because its instances and their network interfaces exist only for the duration of a session.

- [Using content audit security group policies with Firewall Manager](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/security-group-policies-audit.html)
- [How to continuously audit and limit security groups with AWS Firewall Manager](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/how-to-continuously-audit-and-limit-security-groups-with-aws-firewall-manager/)
- [What is Network Access Analyzer?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/network-access-analyzer/what-is-network-access-analyzer.html)

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.CapacityProvider.10](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlcapacityprovider10)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.CapacityProvider.10](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlcapacityprovider10)): This implementation guidance recommends restricting the inbound and outbound rules on your capacity provider's security groups to the required addresses, protocols, and ports. Excluding unrestricted addresses such as 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 from those inbound and outbound rules helps reduce the network exposure of your capacity provider's instances.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.CodeInterpreter.1

*Service control policy (SCP) — Preventive*

Governs the IAM permissions below.

| Actions | Resources | Condition keys |
|---|---|---|
| `*` | `*` | `aws:PrincipalTag/dp:exclude:network`, `aws:PrincipalTag/dp:include:network`, `aws:SourceIp`, `aws:SourceVpc` (alternatives: `aws:SourceVpce`), `aws:ViaAWSService` |
| `*` | `*` | `aws:RequestedRegion`, `aws:SourceVpc` |

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.CodeInterpreter.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlcodeinterpreter1)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.CodeInterpreter.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlcodeinterpreter1)): This implementation guidance recommends applying the `aws:PrincipalTag/dp:include:network`, `aws:SourceIp`, and `aws:SourceVpc` condition keys in a service control policy (SCP), pairing `aws:SourceVpc` with `aws:RequestedRegion`. These conditions help restrict requests made with your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore code interpreter's execution role credentials to expected networks, while exempting AWS services that call through forward access sessions (`aws:ViaAWSService`). Apply the tag only to the execution role of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore code interpreters whose `$.networkConfiguration.networkMode`, the code interpreter's network mode, is `VPC`, because in `PUBLIC` or `SANDBOX` network mode a code interpreter's requests originate from an AWS-managed network, outside your expected networks.

**Data perimeter** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.CodeInterpreter.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlcodeinterpreter1)): The default network perimeter service control policy (SCP) samples restrict calls to expected networks for IAM principals tagged with `dp:include:network` set to `true`. Tag your code interpreter's IAM execution role this way to bring calls made with its credentials into your network perimeter. If the execution role assumes another role as part of its operations, also restrict that assumed role to expected networks.
- [SCP sample: network perimeter policy with aws:SourceVpc](https://github.com/aws-samples/data-perimeter-policy-examples/blob/main/service_control_policies/network_perimeter_sourcevpc_scp.json)
- [SCP sample: network perimeter policy with aws:VpceOrgID](https://github.com/aws-samples/data-perimeter-policy-examples/blob/main/service_control_policies/network_perimeter_vpceorgid_scp.json)
- [Network perimeter guidance for the data perimeter SCP examples](https://github.com/aws-samples/data-perimeter-policy-examples/blob/main/service_control_policies/README.md#sidenforcenetworkperimetervpceorgid)

**Reference:** To restrict access to expected networks at scale, use the `aws:VpceOrgID`, `aws:VpceOrgPaths`, or `aws:VpceAccount` condition keys where supported. These scope access to VPC endpoints owned by accounts within a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. These keys are preferred for enforcing network perimeter controls across multiple accounts because they do not require you to enumerate individual VPCs or endpoints. For finer-grained control, use the `aws:SourceVpc` or `aws:SourceVpce` condition keys to restrict access to a specific VPC or VPC endpoint. Use them also for services that do not currently support the `aws:VpceOrgID`, `aws:VpceOrgPaths`, or `aws:VpceAccount` condition keys. Because VPC IDs are unique only within a Region, pair `aws:SourceVpc` with `aws:RequestedRegion`. Use `aws:SourceIp` with your public IP ranges for requests that do not traverse a VPC endpoint. Use `aws:ViaAWSService` to exempt AWS services that call with your credentials through forward access sessions (FAS). Use `aws:PrincipalTag/tag-key` to apply the restriction to principals whose credentials can be used outside your expected networks, tagged with the selected key and value. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.
- [Establishing a network perimeter](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies_data-perimeters.html#access_policies_data-perimeters-network)
- [SCP sample: network perimeter policy with aws:VpceOrgID](https://github.com/aws-samples/data-perimeter-policy-examples/blob/main/service_control_policies/network_perimeter_vpceorgid_scp.json)

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.CodeInterpreter.2

*CloudFormation hook — Proactive*

Validates template properties before provisioning.

- `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::CodeInterpreterCustom`: `$.ExecutionRoleArn`

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.CodeInterpreter.2](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlcodeinterpreter2)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.CodeInterpreter.2](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlcodeinterpreter2)): This implementation guidance recommends validating the trust policy of `$.ExecutionRoleArn`, your code interpreter's execution role, including source conditions on service principals, before provisioning. This helps prevent the code interpreter from being provisioned when that trust policy can grant public access, or role assumption beyond the reference policy you maintain.

**Reference:** This implementation recommends using IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks.

Custom policy checks (`CheckNoPublicAccess`, `CheckNoNewAccess`) use automated reasoning to provide a higher level of assurance. They provably verify that a policy does not grant public access or grant new access beyond a reference policy you maintain.

The first reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` allowlists the principals this role's trust policy may grant assumption to. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption beyond that allowlist. Example reference policies for role trust policies are available in the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples repository.

The second reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` encodes the source conditions you accept when the service principal assumes the role: one role-assumption statement per accepted combination of the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, with placeholders for your account, organization, and resource values. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption that no statement of the reference allows, including grants that omit the condition keys or weaken them with `IfExists`.
- [IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access-analyzer-custom-policy-checks.html)
- [IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples](https://github.com/aws-samples/iam-access-analyzer-custom-policy-check-samples)

3. Call `iam:GetRole` with `$.RoleName`; check `$.Role.AssumeRolePolicyDocument`

5. Call `accessanalyzer:CheckNoNewAccess` with `$.newPolicyDocument`, `$.existingPolicyDocument`, `$.policyType` = `RESOURCE_POLICY`; check `$.result`

These conditions help prevent principals outside your organization from assuming your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore code interpreter's execution role, `$.executionRoleArn`.

**Reference:** To restrict access to trusted identities, use the `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`, or `aws:PrincipalAccount` condition keys. These scope access to IAM principals within a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. These keys do not contain your organization or account values for requests by AWS service principals, so apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `false`. As a defense-in-depth measure, use the `aws:SourceOrgID`, `aws:SourceOrgPaths`, `aws:SourceAccount`, or `aws:SourceArn` condition keys to restrict service access to your roles. These scope access performed on behalf of resources within a particular organization, specific organizational units, a specific AWS account, or a particular resource, respectively. Apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `true`. Also require that `aws:SourceAccount` is present in the request context, because not every service integration populates these keys. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.
