### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.CodeInterpreter.10

*Guidance — Directive*

This guidance applies to custom code interpreters that set `$.networkConfiguration.networkMode` to `VPC`. When you call `CreateCodeInterpreter`, list two or more subnets in different Availability Zones (AZs) in `$.networkConfiguration.vpcConfig.subnets[*]`. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore creates elastic network interfaces (ENIs) in those subnets through the `AWSServiceRoleForBedrockAgentCoreNetwork` service-linked role. Subnets in different AZs let AgentCore place your code interpreter's ENIs in more than one AZ. This helps your code interpreter's VPC connectivity survive the loss of a single AZ. If your code interpreter mounts Amazon EFS or Amazon S3 Files access points, create a mount target in each AZ that your subnets use.

Each subnet belongs to one AZ, so the code interpreter's AZ coverage depends on the subnets you choose. Before you supply subnet IDs, call the Amazon EC2 `DescribeSubnets` operation and confirm that their `AvailabilityZone` values differ. Also check each `AvailabilityZoneId` against the AZs that AgentCore supports for VPC connectivity in your Region. Subnets in unsupported AZs cause code interpreter creation to fail. Code interpreters have no update operation, so the subnet list is fixed at creation. In AWS CloudFormation, changing the `Subnets` property of `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::CodeInterpreterCustom` requires replacing the resource. Standardize on infrastructure-as-code review of the templates and modules that create code interpreters. Confirm that each one supplies at least two subnets from different AZs. To correct an existing code interpreter, create a replacement with a corrected subnet list. Stop the original's active sessions before you delete it.

To verify the deployed state, call `GetCodeInterpreter` and note the subnets in `$.networkConfiguration.vpcConfig.subnets[*]` and the security groups it returns. Then call the Amazon EC2 `DescribeNetworkInterfaces` operation, filtering by those subnet and security group IDs. If your account's managed resource visibility is hidden, set `IncludeManagedResources` to `true` so the results can include ENIs that AgentCore provisions. Confirm that the returned ENIs span more than one AZ. AgentCore shares ENIs across agents that use the same subnet and security group configuration, so a returned ENI might also serve other resources.

To assess and track multi-AZ posture at scale, use AWS Resilience Hub. Include your code interpreter's application resources in a Resilience Hub application and run a resiliency assessment. The assessment can flag single-AZ concentration against your resiliency policy. The Resilience Hub list of supported services doesn't include Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Confirm what your assessment covers. Keep the subnet and ENI checks as your direct verification for the code interpreter.

- [Subnets for your VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/configure-subnets.html)
- [DescribeSubnets (Amazon EC2 API Reference)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/APIReference/API_DescribeSubnets.html)
- [What is AWS Resilience Hub?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/resilience-hub/latest/userguide/what-is.html)

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.CodeInterpreter.4](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlcodeinterpreter4)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.CodeInterpreter.4](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlcodeinterpreter4)): This implementation guidance recommends supplying two or more subnets from different Availability Zones in `$.networkConfiguration.vpcConfig.subnets[*]`, the subnets of your custom code interpreter's VPC configuration. Spreading the elastic network interfaces that Amazon Bedrock AgentCore creates for your code interpreter across zones helps its VPC connectivity survive the loss of a single Availability Zone.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.CodeInterpreter.16

*Guidance — Directive*

This guidance applies to custom code interpreters that use `VPC` network mode. Configure their security groups following least-privilege best practices. These are the groups you specify in `$.networkConfiguration.vpcConfig.securityGroups[*]` when you call `CreateCodeInterpreter`. AgentCore attaches them to the elastic network interfaces it creates in your subnets. Their rules help control which VPC resources, AWS service endpoints, and NAT-routed internet destinations your code interpreter sessions can communicate with.

Restrict both inbound and outbound rules to only the required sources and destinations (IP address ranges, referenced security groups, or prefix lists), protocols, and ports. Avoid rules that allow unrestricted access from or to 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0, particularly on administrative or sensitive ports. A new security group includes an outbound rule that allows all outbound traffic. Replace that rule with outbound rules for only the destinations your sessions need. When the peer is an AWS resource in a security group, reference that security group instead of its address range. Examples of such peers include a database or a file system mount target in your VPC. The rule then follows the peer's network interfaces rather than addresses that can change.

You can't change which security groups a code interpreter uses after you create it. Define least-privilege groups before you call `CreateCodeInterpreter`. You can still tighten the rules in those groups later. Rule changes apply automatically to all resources associated with the group. To use different groups, recreate the code interpreter.

To govern security groups at scale, use AWS Firewall Manager security group policies across your organization in AWS Organizations. You can scope these policies by account, organizational unit (OU), or tag. A common security group policy applies a baseline security group. A content audit security group policy audits inbound and outbound rules against an allow list or a block list. It flags noncompliant groups in a central dashboard, notifies you, and can automatically remediate noncompliant rules. A usage audit security group policy removes unused or redundant security groups. Include the Amazon VPC security group resource type in your content audit policy scope. This brings the groups your code interpreter uses into scope, even though AgentCore creates and manages the network interfaces they attach to. Before you rely on a common policy, confirm that it can apply to the network interfaces that AgentCore manages.

To verify unintended access that your security groups permit, use Amazon VPC Network Access Analyzer. Define a Network Access Scope for the access you consider unintended. For example, match any path that reaches administrative ports 22 or 3389 from an unrestricted address. You can also match outbound paths from your code interpreter's network interfaces to an internet gateway when you don't intend internet access. Create the scope by calling `CreateNetworkInsightsAccessScope`. Run an analysis by calling `StartNetworkInsightsAccessScopeAnalysis`, and then review the findings. Network Access Analyzer evaluates your security groups together with route tables, network ACLs, and public IP assignment. This helps you identify unintended network access relative to your security requirements.

- [Using content audit security group policies with Firewall Manager](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/security-group-policies-audit.html)
- [How to continuously audit and limit security groups with AWS Firewall Manager](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/how-to-continuously-audit-and-limit-security-groups-with-aws-firewall-manager/)
- [What is Network Access Analyzer?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/network-access-analyzer/what-is-network-access-analyzer.html)

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.CodeInterpreter.6](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlcodeinterpreter6)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.CodeInterpreter.6](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlcodeinterpreter6)): This implementation guidance recommends restricting the inbound and outbound rules on your code interpreter's security groups to the required addresses, protocols, and ports. Excluding unrestricted addresses such as 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 from those inbound and outbound rules helps reduce the network exposure of your code interpreter.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.ConsentPortal.1

*CloudFormation hook — Proactive*

Validates template properties before provisioning.

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.ConsentPortal.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlconsentportal1)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.ConsentPortal.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlconsentportal1)): This implementation guidance recommends validating the trust policy of `$.ExecutionRoleArn`, your consent portal's execution role, including source conditions on service principals, before provisioning. This helps prevent the consent portal from being provisioned when that trust policy can grant public access, or role assumption beyond the reference policy you maintain.

**Reference:** This implementation recommends using IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks. Custom policy checks (`CheckNoPublicAccess`, `CheckNoNewAccess`) use automated reasoning to provide a higher level of assurance. They provably verify that a policy does not grant public access or grant new access beyond a reference policy you maintain. The first reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` allowlists the principals this role's trust policy may grant assumption to. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption beyond that allowlist. Example reference policies for role trust policies are available in the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples repository. The second reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` encodes the source conditions you accept when the service principal assumes the role: one sts:AssumeRole statement per accepted combination of the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, with placeholders for your account, organization, and resource values. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption that no statement of the reference allows, including grants that omit the condition keys or weaken them with `IfExists`.
- [IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access-analyzer-custom-policy-checks.html)
- [IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples](https://github.com/aws-samples/iam-access-analyzer-custom-policy-check-samples)

3. Call `iam:GetRole` with `$.RoleName`; check `$.Role.AssumeRolePolicyDocument`
4. Call `accessanalyzer:CheckNoPublicAccess` with `$.policyDocument`, `$.resourceType` = `AWS::IAM::AssumeRolePolicyDocument`; check `$.result`
5. Call `accessanalyzer:CheckNoNewAccess` with `$.newPolicyDocument`, `$.existingPolicyDocument`, `$.policyType` = `RESOURCE_POLICY`; check `$.result`
6. Call `accessanalyzer:CheckNoNewAccess` with `$.newPolicyDocument`, `$.existingPolicyDocument`, `$.policyType` = `RESOURCE_POLICY`; check `$.result`

Flagging trust policies that allow public role assumption, or assumption beyond your reference policy, or that omit the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, helps you detect overly permissive role assumption.

**Reference:** This implementation recommends using IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption that no statement of the reference allows, including grants that omit the condition keys or weaken them with `IfExists`.

| Principal | Actions | Condition keys |
|---|---|---|
| `bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com` | `sts:AssumeRole` | `aws:SourceAccount` (alternatives: `aws:SourceOrgID`, `aws:SourceOrgPaths`), `aws:SourceArn` |

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.ConsentPortal.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlconsentportal1)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.ConsentPortal.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlconsentportal1)): This implementation guidance recommends a trust policy that restricts assumption of your consent portal's execution role, `$.executionRoleArn`, to the `bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com` service principal with the `aws:SourceArn` and `aws:SourceAccount` condition keys. These conditions help prevent Amazon Bedrock AgentCore from assuming the role on behalf of consent portals outside the sources you specify.

**Reference:** Confirm that IAM role trust policies grant access only to the AWS service principals you intend. Review the `Principal` element of each policy and verify it names only the service principals your workload requires. As a defense-in-depth measure, use the `aws:SourceOrgID`, `aws:SourceOrgPaths`, `aws:SourceAccount`, or `aws:SourceArn` condition keys. These scope access performed on behalf of resources within a particular organization, specific organizational units, a specific AWS account, or a particular resource, respectively. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.
- [Establishing an identity perimeter](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies_data-perimeters.html#access_policies_data-perimeters-identity)

*Resource control policy (RCP) — Preventive*

Governs the IAM permissions below.

| Actions | Resources | Condition keys |
|---|---|---|
| `sts:AssumeRole` | `*` | `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`, `aws:PrincipalOrgID` (alternatives: `aws:PrincipalAccount`, `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`) |
| `sts:AssumeRole` | `*` | `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID` (alternatives: `aws:SourceOrgPaths`) |

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.ConsentPortal.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlconsentportal1)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.ConsentPortal.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlconsentportal1)): This implementation guidance recommends restricting `sts:AssumeRole` with the `aws:PrincipalOrgID` condition key in a resource control policy (RCP), while exempting AWS services acting on your behalf (`aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`) and scoping those service requests with `aws:SourceOrgID`. These conditions help prevent principals outside your organization from assuming your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore consent portal's execution role, `$.executionRoleArn`.

**Reference:** To restrict access to trusted identities, use the `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`, or `aws:PrincipalAccount` condition keys. These scope access to IAM principals within a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. These keys do not contain your organization or account values for requests by AWS service principals, so apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `false`. As a defense-in-depth measure, use the `aws:SourceOrgID`, `aws:SourceOrgPaths`, `aws:SourceAccount`, or `aws:SourceArn` condition keys to restrict service access to your roles. These scope access performed on behalf of resources within a particular organization, specific organizational units, a specific AWS account, or a particular resource, respectively. Apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `true`. Also require that `aws:SourceAccount` is present in the request context, because not every service integration populates these keys. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Gateway.1

*CloudFormation hook — Proactive*

Validates template properties before provisioning.

- `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Gateway`: `$.RoleArn`

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Gateway.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlgateway1)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Gateway.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlgateway1)): This implementation guidance recommends validating the trust policy of `$.RoleArn`, your gateway's service role, including source conditions on service principals, before provisioning. This helps prevent the gateway from being provisioned when that trust policy can grant public access, or role assumption beyond the reference policy you maintain.

**Reference:** This implementation recommends using IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks.

Custom policy checks (`CheckNoPublicAccess`, `CheckNoNewAccess`) use automated reasoning to provide a higher level of assurance. They provably verify that a policy does not grant public access or grant new access beyond a reference policy you maintain.

The first reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` allowlists the principals this role's trust policy may grant assumption to. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption beyond that allowlist. Example reference policies for role trust policies are available in the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples repository.

The second reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` encodes the source conditions you accept when the service principal assumes the role: one role-assumption statement per accepted combination of the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, with placeholders for your account, organization, and resource values. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption that no statement of the reference allows, including grants that omit the condition keys or weaken them with `IfExists`.
- [IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access-analyzer-custom-policy-checks.html)
- [IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples](https://github.com/aws-samples/iam-access-analyzer-custom-policy-check-samples)

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Gateway.2

*AWS Config rule — Detective*

A periodic rule that evaluates via the API operation chain below.

1. Call `bedrock-agentcore-control:ListGateways`; check `$.items[*].gatewayId`
2. Call `bedrock-agentcore-control:GetGateway` with `$.gatewayIdentifier`; check `$.roleArn`
3. Call `iam:GetRole` with `$.RoleName`; check `$.Role.AssumeRolePolicyDocument`
4. Call `accessanalyzer:CheckNoPublicAccess` with `$.policyDocument`, `$.resourceType` = `AWS::IAM::AssumeRolePolicyDocument`; check `$.result`
5. Call `accessanalyzer:CheckNoNewAccess` with `$.newPolicyDocument`, `$.existingPolicyDocument`, `$.policyType` = `RESOURCE_POLICY`; check `$.result`
6. Call `accessanalyzer:CheckNoNewAccess` with `$.newPolicyDocument`, `$.existingPolicyDocument`, `$.policyType` = `RESOURCE_POLICY`; check `$.result`

Flagging trust policies that allow public role assumption, or assumption beyond your reference policy, or that omit the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, helps you detect overly permissive role assumption.

**Reference:** This implementation recommends using IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks.

Custom policy checks (`CheckNoPublicAccess`, `CheckNoNewAccess`) use automated reasoning to provide a higher level of assurance. They provably verify that a policy does not grant public access or grant new access beyond a reference policy you maintain.

The first reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` allowlists the principals this role's trust policy may grant assumption to. The second reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` encodes the source conditions you accept when the service principal assumes the role: one role-assumption statement per accepted combination of the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, with placeholders for your account, organization, and resource values. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption that no statement of the reference allows, including grants that omit the condition keys or weaken them with `IfExists`.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Gateway.13

*Guidance — Directive*

Your gateway's `CUSTOM_JWT` authorizer can reach a private (VPC-hosted) identity provider through a managed private endpoint. In that configuration, supply two or more subnets from different Availability Zones (AZs) in `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds[*]` when you call `CreateGateway` or `UpdateGateway`. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore places a managed VPC Lattice resource gateway in these subnets, with an elastic network interface (ENI) in each subnet. AgentCore uses these ENIs to reach your identity provider's OIDC discovery and JWKS endpoints. Spreading the ENIs across zones helps that connectivity survive the loss of a single Availability Zone.

Each subnet resides entirely within one Availability Zone. The subnets you choose therefore define the endpoint's zone footprint. Before you supply subnet IDs, call `DescribeSubnets` and confirm from the `AvailabilityZone` field that the subnets belong to distinct Availability Zones. Also confirm that your identity provider's OIDC discovery and JWKS endpoints are reachable from every subnet you supply. Standardize on infrastructure-as-code review so that templates and modules that create or update the gateway supply at least two such subnets.

To verify the deployed state, call `GetGateway` and review the subnet IDs returned in its authorizer configuration. You can also call `DescribeNetworkInterfaces` with a `subnet-id` filter for those subnets. Confirm that the resource gateway's network interfaces span more than one Availability Zone.

To assess and track multi-AZ posture at scale, you can include your gateway's application resources in an AWS Resilience Hub application. Then run a resiliency assessment, which can flag single-AZ concentration against your resiliency policy. Resilience Hub does not currently list Amazon Bedrock AgentCore or Amazon VPC Lattice among its supported services. Confirm coverage before you rely on its findings for this endpoint.

- [Subnets for your VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/configure-subnets.html)
- [DescribeSubnets (Amazon EC2 API Reference)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/APIReference/API_DescribeSubnets.html)
- [What is AWS Resilience Hub?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/resilience-hub/latest/userguide/what-is.html)

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Gateway.6](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlgateway6)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Gateway.6](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlgateway6)): This implementation guidance recommends supplying two or more subnets from different Availability Zones in `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds[*]`, the subnet IDs of your gateway's identity provider managed private endpoint. Spreading the network interfaces of the VPC Lattice resource gateway that AgentCore creates across zones helps connectivity to your private identity provider survive the loss of a single Availability Zone.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Gateway.16

| Actions | Resources | Condition keys |

As a result, principals outside the accounts you name are restricted from invoking your gateway, even when they can reach its invocation URL. This guidance applies to an AgentCore gateway whose callers authenticate as IAM principals (SigV4). An AgentCore gateway configured with OAuth authentication must name a wildcard principal instead, so this guidance does not apply to it.

**Reference:** Confirm that resource-based policies grant access only to authorized identities. As a defense-in-depth measure, use the `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`, or `aws:PrincipalAccount` condition keys to restrict access to trusted identities. These scope access to IAM principals within a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Gateway.9](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlgateway9)): This implementation guidance recommends validating `$.AuthorizerConfiguration.CustomJWTAuthorizer.DiscoveryUrl`, the identity provider discovery URL for inbound JWT authorization, before provisioning. That check helps prevent an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway from being provisioned with an identity provider's issuer path outside your organization's trust boundary.

**Data perimeter** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Gateway.9](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlgateway9)): Within your resource perimeter, a CloudFormation Hook can help prevent developers from specifying a gateway authorizer that trusts an identity provider outside your organization. The hook confirms that `$.AuthorizerConfiguration.CustomJWTAuthorizer.DiscoveryUrl` matches the full discovery URL, host and path, of an identity provider you trust before the gateway is provisioned. For example, Amazon Cognito user pools that use the default issuer share one regional host (`cognito-idp.<region>.amazonaws.com`). These pools differ only in the user-pool-ID segment of the path. A host-only comparison would therefore admit every such pool in the Region.

| Actions | Resources | Condition keys |

| `bedrock-agentcore:*` | `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:gateway/${GatewayId}` | `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`, `aws:PrincipalOrgID` (alternatives: `aws:PrincipalAccount`, `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`) |
| `bedrock-agentcore:*` | `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:gateway/${GatewayId}` | `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID` (alternatives: `aws:SourceOrgPaths`) |

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Gateway.10](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlgateway10)): This implementation guidance recommends governing Amazon Bedrock AgentCore API calls against your gateway with the `aws:PrincipalOrgID` condition key in its resource-based policy, while exempting AWS services that access it on your behalf (`aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`) and scoping those service requests with `aws:SourceOrgID`. These conditions help prevent identities outside your organization from accessing your gateway.

**Reference:** Confirm that resource-based policies grant access only to trusted identities and to services acting on your behalf. As a defense-in-depth measure, use the `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`, or `aws:PrincipalAccount` condition keys to restrict access to trusted identities. These scope access to IAM principals within a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. These keys do not contain your organization or account values for requests by AWS service principals, so apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `false`. To restrict service access to your resources, use the `aws:SourceOrgID`, `aws:SourceOrgPaths`, `aws:SourceAccount`, or `aws:SourceArn` condition keys. These scope access performed on behalf of resources within a particular organization, specific organizational units, a specific AWS account, or a particular resource, respectively. Apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `true`. Also require that `aws:SourceAccount` is present in the request context, because not every service integration populates these keys. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.
- [Establishing an identity perimeter](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies_data-perimeters.html#access_policies_data-perimeters-identity)

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Gateway.24

*CloudFormation hook — Proactive*

Validates template properties before provisioning.

- `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::ResourcePolicy`: `$.Policy`

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Gateway.10](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlgateway10)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Gateway.10](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlgateway10)): This implementation guidance recommends validating `$.Policy`, the resource-based policy that controls who can invoke your gateway, before provisioning your AgentCore gateway's resource policy. The hook helps prevent a policy that can grant access beyond your reference policy, permissions you specify such as `bedrock-agentcore:InvokeGateway`, or access to an AWS service principal beyond a reference policy containing the source conditions you accept from being provisioned.

**Reference:** This implementation recommends using IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks. Custom policy checks (`CheckNoNewAccess`, `CheckAccessNotGranted`) use automated reasoning to provide a higher level of assurance. They provably verify that a policy does not grant new access beyond a reference policy you maintain or grant specified permissions. The first reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` allowlists the principals that may be granted access to the resource. The check fails when the resource-based policy grants access beyond that allowlist. Example reference policies for resource-based policies are available in the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples repository. The second reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` encodes the source conditions you accept on grants to an AWS service principal: one statement per accepted combination of the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, with placeholders for your account, organization, and resource values. The check fails when the policy grants a service principal access that no statement of the reference allows, including grants that omit the condition keys or weaken them with `IfExists`.
- [IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access-analyzer-custom-policy-checks.html)
- [IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples](https://github.com/aws-samples/iam-access-analyzer-custom-policy-check-samples)

3. Call `bedrock-agentcore-control:GetResourcePolicy` with `$.resourceArn`; check `$.policy`
4. Call `accessanalyzer:CheckNoNewAccess` with `$.newPolicyDocument`, `$.existingPolicyDocument`, `$.policyType` = `RESOURCE_POLICY`; check `$.result`
5. Call `accessanalyzer:CheckAccessNotGranted` with `$.policyDocument`, `$.policyType` = `RESOURCE_POLICY`, `$.access[*].actions[*]`; check `$.result`
6. Call `accessanalyzer:CheckNoNewAccess` with `$.newPolicyDocument`, `$.existingPolicyDocument`, `$.policyType` = `RESOURCE_POLICY`; check `$.result`

The check fails when the policy grants a service principal access that no statement of the reference allows, including grants that omit the condition keys or weaken them with `IfExists`.

As a result, requests made on behalf of a resource or account you have not designated are restricted from invoking your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway.

**Reference:** To restrict service access to your resources, use the `aws:SourceOrgID`, `aws:SourceOrgPaths`, `aws:SourceAccount`, or `aws:SourceArn` condition keys. These scope access performed on behalf of resources within a particular organization, specific organizational units, a specific AWS account, or a particular resource, respectively. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

**Reference:** This implementation recommends using IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks. Custom policy checks (`CheckNoNewAccess`) use automated reasoning to provide a higher level of assurance. They provably verify that a policy does not grant new access beyond a reference policy you maintain. The reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` encodes the source conditions you accept on grants to an AWS service principal: one statement per accepted combination of the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, with placeholders for your account, organization, and resource values. The check fails when the policy grants a service principal access that no statement of the reference allows, including grants that omit the condition keys or weaken them with `IfExists`. The IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples repository shows the reference policy format; compose the policy from the key combinations you accept.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Gateway.33

*Guidance — Directive*

When your gateway uses a `CUSTOM_JWT` authorizer with a private (VPC-hosted) identity provider, AgentCore reaches it through a private endpoint. With a managed VPC resource, AgentCore associates the security groups you list in `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]` with a VPC Lattice resource gateway in your VPC. If you don't specify any, the default security group for the VPC is used. That group's rules then govern traffic to your identity provider.

Configure these security groups following least-privilege best practices. Restrict inbound and outbound rules to only the required sources and destinations (IP address ranges, referenced security groups, or prefix lists), protocols, and ports. For this gateway, the required traffic is typically HTTPS on port 443 to your identity provider's OIDC discovery, JWKS, and token endpoints. Avoid rules that permit unrestricted access from or to any IP address (0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0). Where the peer is an AWS resource in a security group, reference that security group instead of its address range. That peer can be your identity provider or an internal load balancer in front of it. The rule then follows the peer's network interfaces rather than addresses that can change. Apply the same least-privilege review to the security groups that govern any additional identity provider domains you configure in `privateEndpointOverrides`.

To govern security groups at scale, use AWS Firewall Manager security group policies across your organization in AWS Organizations. You can scope each policy by account, organizational unit (OU), or tag. A common policy applies a baseline group. A content audit policy audits inbound and outbound rules against an allow-list or block-list. It flags non-compliant groups in a central dashboard, notifies you, and can auto-remediate. Review its findings before you turn on automatic remediation. A usage audit policy removes unused or redundant groups. The managed resource gateway is read-only to you. Target the security groups you supply, for example with a content audit policy that covers Amazon VPC security groups.

To verify unintended access permitted by your security groups, use Amazon VPC Network Access Analyzer. Define a Network Access Scope for the access you consider unintended. For example, match any path that reaches administrative ports 22 or 3389 from an unrestricted address. You can reference the security groups you supply by ID as a path source or destination. Create the scope with `CreateNetworkInsightsAccessScope`, start an analysis with `StartNetworkInsightsAccessScopeAnalysis`, and review the findings. Network Access Analyzer reasons about the security group together with the route table, network ACL, and public IP assignment. This helps you identify unintended network access relative to your security and compliance requirements.

- [Using content audit security group policies with Firewall Manager](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/security-group-policies-audit.html)
- [How to continuously audit and limit security groups with AWS Firewall Manager](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/how-to-continuously-audit-and-limit-security-groups-with-aws-firewall-manager/)
- [What is Network Access Analyzer?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/network-access-analyzer/what-is-network-access-analyzer.html)

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Gateway.14](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlgateway14)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Gateway.14](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlgateway14)): This implementation guidance recommends restricting the inbound and outbound rules on the security groups in `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]`, the groups on the VPC Lattice resource gateway that carries traffic to your identity provider, to the required addresses, protocols, and ports. Excluding unrestricted addresses such as 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 from those inbound and outbound rules helps reduce the network exposure of your gateway's identity provider private endpoint.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.GatewayTarget.6

*Guidance — Directive*

For gateway targets that use a managed private endpoint, supply two or more subnets from different Availability Zones in `$.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds[*]`. Set this list when you call `CreateGatewayTarget` or `UpdateGatewayTarget`. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore places the target's managed VPC Lattice resource gateway in those subnets. The resource gateway is a wrapper around elastic network interfaces (ENIs) in your VPC. Each subnet resides in a single Availability Zone. A one-subnet list therefore puts every interface in the same zone. Spreading the ENIs across zones helps your target's private connectivity survive the loss of a single Availability Zone.

Subnet-to-zone membership is a property of each subnet, not of the gateway target. Before you supply subnet IDs, call `DescribeSubnets` and confirm from the `AvailabilityZone` field that the subnets belong to distinct Availability Zones. Also confirm from the `AvailabilityZoneId` field that each subnet is in a zone that AgentCore Gateway supports for managed private endpoints in your Region. Standardize on infrastructure-as-code review for the templates and modules that create your gateway targets. Each review should confirm that the template supplies at least two subnets from different zones. In AWS CloudFormation, this list is the `SubnetIds` property of `ManagedVpcResource` in an `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::GatewayTarget` resource.

To verify the deployed state, call `GetGatewayTarget`. The response echoes the configured subnets and returns the ARN of the managed resource gateway. Confirm that those subnets span more than one Availability Zone. You can also list the resource gateway's network interfaces with `DescribeNetworkInterfaces` and confirm that their subnets span more than one zone.

To assess and track Availability Zone resilience at scale, use AWS Resilience Hub. Add your application's resources to a Resilience Hub application and run a resiliency assessment. The assessment measures resiliency against the targets your resiliency policy sets for Availability Zone disruptions. Coverage depends on the resource types that Resilience Hub supports. Where it does not assess your gateway target directly, include the supported resources behind your private endpoint. Examples include an internal load balancer, a private Amazon API Gateway API, or backend compute.

- [Subnets for your VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/configure-subnets.html)
- [DescribeSubnets (Amazon EC2 API Reference)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/APIReference/API_DescribeSubnets.html)
- [What is AWS Resilience Hub?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/resilience-hub/latest/userguide/what-is.html)

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.GatewayTarget.3](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlgatewaytarget3)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.GatewayTarget.3](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlgatewaytarget3)): This implementation guidance recommends supplying two or more subnets from different Availability Zones in `$.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds[*]`, the subnets of your gateway target's managed private endpoint. Spreading the network interfaces AgentCore creates for the endpoint's VPC Lattice resource gateway across zones helps private connectivity survive the loss of a single Availability Zone.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.GatewayTarget.12

*Guidance — Directive*

Follow least-privilege best practices for the security groups that you specify in `$.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]` when you call `CreateGatewayTarget` or `UpdateGatewayTarget`. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore associates these groups with the managed VPC Lattice resource gateway that it places in your subnets. Their outbound rules control traffic from the resource gateway to your private resource, such as an MCP server or REST API. Restrict both inbound and outbound rules to only the required sources and destinations (IP address ranges, referenced security groups, or prefix lists), protocols, and ports. For example, allow outbound traffic only to your private resource on the port that it listens on, typically 443 for HTTPS. If you route traffic through an intermediate domain, such as a VPC endpoint or internal load balancer, allow traffic to that component instead. Avoid rules that permit unrestricted access from or to any address, such as 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0. Where the peer is an AWS resource in a security group, reference that security group instead of its address range. The rule then follows the peer's network interfaces rather than addresses that can change. If you don't specify any security groups, AgentCore uses the default security group for the VPC. Its default rules allow all outbound IPv4 traffic, plus IPv6 traffic when the VPC has an IPv6 CIDR block. Specify security groups with restricted rules instead of relying on the default security group.

To govern security groups at scale, use AWS Firewall Manager security group policies across your organization in AWS Organizations. You can scope these policies by account, organizational unit (OU), or tag. A common security group policy applies a baseline security group. A content audit security group policy audits inbound and outbound rules against an allow list or a deny list. It flags noncompliant groups in a central dashboard, sends notifications, and can automatically remediate noncompliant rules. A usage audit security group policy identifies unused or redundant security groups and can remove them. You can't modify the managed resource gateway. Policy actions that change its security group associations might not apply to it. Content audit policies can still evaluate the rules in the security groups that you create and specify. Review the findings before you enable automatic remediation. Automatic remediation can remove a rule that the connection to your private resource requires.

To verify unintended access that your security groups permit, use Amazon VPC Network Access Analyzer. Define a Network Access Scope for the access that you consider unintended. For example, match any path that reaches administrative ports 22 or 3389 from an unrestricted address. For a gateway target, you can also match paths that start at the resource gateway's security groups and exclude paths that end at your private resource. Create the scope by calling `CreateNetworkInsightsAccessScope`, start an analysis by calling `StartNetworkInsightsAccessScopeAnalysis`, and review the findings. Network Access Analyzer evaluates the security group together with the route table, network ACL, and public IP assignment. This helps you identify unintended network access relative to your security and compliance requirements.

- [Using content audit security group policies with Firewall Manager](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/security-group-policies-audit.html)
- [How to continuously audit and limit security groups with AWS Firewall Manager](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/how-to-continuously-audit-and-limit-security-groups-with-aws-firewall-manager/)
- [What is Network Access Analyzer?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/network-access-analyzer/what-is-network-access-analyzer.html)

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.GatewayTarget.5](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlgatewaytarget5)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.GatewayTarget.5](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlgatewaytarget5)): This implementation guidance recommends restricting the inbound and outbound rules on the security groups in `$.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]`, the groups associated with your gateway target's managed VPC Lattice resource gateway, to the required addresses, protocols, and ports. Excluding unrestricted addresses such as 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 from those inbound and outbound rules helps reduce the network exposure of the resource gateway's network interfaces.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Harness.1

*Service control policy (SCP) — Preventive*

Governs the IAM permissions below.

| Actions | Resources | Condition keys |
|---|---|---|
| `*` | `*` | `aws:PrincipalTag/dp:exclude:network`, `aws:PrincipalTag/dp:include:network`, `aws:SourceIp`, `aws:SourceVpc` (alternatives: `aws:SourceVpce`), `aws:ViaAWSService` |
| `*` | `*` | `aws:RequestedRegion`, `aws:SourceVpc` |

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Harness.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlharness1)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Harness.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlharness1)): This implementation guidance recommends applying the `aws:PrincipalTag/dp:include:network`, `aws:SourceIp`, and `aws:SourceVpc` condition keys in a service control policy (SCP), pairing `aws:SourceVpc` with `aws:RequestedRegion`. These conditions help restrict requests made with your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness's execution role credentials to expected networks, while exempting AWS services that call through forward access sessions (`aws:ViaAWSService`). Apply the tag only to the execution role of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harnesses whose `$.environment.agentCoreRuntimeEnvironment.networkConfiguration.networkMode`, the harness network mode, is `VPC`, because in `PUBLIC` network mode a harness's requests originate from an AWS-managed network, outside your expected networks.

**Reference:** To restrict access to expected networks at scale, use the `aws:VpceOrgID`, `aws:VpceOrgPaths`, or `aws:VpceAccount` condition keys where supported. These scope access to VPC endpoints owned by accounts within a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. These keys are preferred for enforcing network perimeter controls across multiple accounts because they do not require you to enumerate individual VPCs or endpoints. For finer-grained control, use the `aws:SourceVpc` or `aws:SourceVpce` condition keys to restrict access to a specific VPC or VPC endpoint. Use them also for services that do not currently support the `aws:VpceOrgID`, `aws:VpceOrgPaths`, or `aws:VpceAccount` condition keys. Because VPC IDs are unique only within a Region, pair `aws:SourceVpc` with `aws:RequestedRegion`. Use `aws:SourceIp` with your public IP ranges for requests that do not traverse a VPC endpoint. Use `aws:ViaAWSService` to exempt AWS services that call with your credentials through forward access sessions (FAS). Use `aws:PrincipalTag/tag-key` to apply the restriction to principals whose credentials can be used outside your expected networks, tagged with the selected key and value. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.
- [Establishing a network perimeter](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies_data-perimeters.html#access_policies_data-perimeters-network)
- [SCP sample: network perimeter policy with aws:VpceOrgID](https://github.com/aws-samples/data-perimeter-policy-examples/blob/main/service_control_policies/network_perimeter_vpceorgid_scp.json)
- [SCP sample: network perimeter policy with aws:SourceVpc](https://github.com/aws-samples/data-perimeter-policy-examples/blob/main/service_control_policies/network_perimeter_sourcevpc_scp.json)

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Harness.2

*CloudFormation hook — Proactive*

Validates template properties before provisioning.

- `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Harness`: `$.ExecutionRoleArn`

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Harness.2](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlharness2)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Harness.2](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlharness2)): This implementation guidance recommends validating the trust policy of `$.ExecutionRoleArn`, your harness's execution role, including source conditions on service principals, before provisioning. This helps prevent the harness from being provisioned when that trust policy can grant public access, or role assumption beyond the reference policy you maintain.

**Reference:** This implementation recommends using IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks. Custom policy checks (`CheckNoPublicAccess`, `CheckNoNewAccess`) use automated reasoning to provide a higher level of assurance. They provably verify that a policy does not grant public access or grant new access beyond a reference policy you maintain. The first reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` allowlists the principals this role's trust policy may grant assumption to. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption beyond that allowlist. Example reference policies for role trust policies are available in the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples repository. The second reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` encodes the source conditions you accept when the service principal assumes the role: one role-assumption statement per accepted combination of the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, with placeholders for your account, organization, and resource values. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption that no statement of the reference allows, including grants that omit the condition keys or weaken them with `IfExists`.
- [IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access-analyzer-custom-policy-checks.html)
- [IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples](https://github.com/aws-samples/iam-access-analyzer-custom-policy-check-samples)

3. Call `iam:GetRole` with `$.RoleName`; check `$.Role.AssumeRolePolicyDocument`
4. Call `accessanalyzer:CheckNoPublicAccess` with `$.policyDocument`, `$.resourceType` = `AWS::IAM::AssumeRolePolicyDocument`; check `$.result`
5. Call `accessanalyzer:CheckNoNewAccess` with `$.newPolicyDocument`, `$.existingPolicyDocument`, `$.policyType` = `RESOURCE_POLICY`; check `$.result`
6. Call `accessanalyzer:CheckNoNewAccess` with `$.newPolicyDocument`, `$.existingPolicyDocument`, `$.policyType` = `RESOURCE_POLICY`; check `$.result`

Flagging trust policies that allow public role assumption, or assumption beyond your reference policy, or that omit the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, helps you detect overly permissive role assumption.

The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption that no statement of the reference allows, including grants that omit the condition keys or weaken them with `IfExists`.

**Reference:** To restrict access to trusted identities, use the `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`, or `aws:PrincipalAccount` condition keys. ### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Harness.9

*Guidance — Directive*

By default, a harness runs on the public network. When you deploy the harness in your VPC with network mode `VPC`, supply two or more subnets that resolve to different Availability Zones. Set them in `$.environment.agentCoreRuntimeEnvironment.networkConfiguration.networkModeConfig.subnets[*]` in your `CreateHarness` and `UpdateHarness` requests. AgentCore creates the elastic network interfaces (ENIs) for your harness's managed AgentCore Runtime in the subnets you specify. Subnets in different zones let AgentCore place those ENIs in more than one Availability Zone. This helps your harness keep VPC connectivity through the loss of a single zone. The subnet list accepts a single subnet, so multi-AZ placement depends on the subnets you supply. If your inbound JWT authorizer reaches a private identity provider through a managed VPC resource, apply the same practice to `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds[*]`. AgentCore Identity places the ENIs of its managed VPC Lattice resource gateway in those subnets.

Each subnet belongs to one Availability Zone, so the zones your harness uses depend on the subnets you choose. Before you supply subnet IDs, call the Amazon EC2 `DescribeSubnets` operation and confirm that they belong to distinct Availability Zones. Check the `AvailabilityZone` and `AvailabilityZoneId` response fields. Also confirm that each Availability Zone ID is one that AgentCore supports for VPC connectivity in your Region. Subnets in unsupported Availability Zones cause resource creation to fail. Standardize on infrastructure-as-code review so that the templates and modules that create harnesses supply at least two subnets from different Availability Zones. This review includes templates that declare `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Harness` resources. If your harness mounts Amazon EFS or Amazon S3 Files access points, create a mount target in each Availability Zone that your harness subnets use. Sessions placed in a zone without a mount target can fail to mount the file system.

To verify the deployed state, call `GetHarness` and resolve the subnets in its runtime network configuration with `DescribeSubnets`. Confirm that those subnets span more than one Availability Zone. Then list the network interfaces in those subnets with the Amazon EC2 `DescribeNetworkInterfaces` operation. Confirm that the attached ENIs exist in more than one Availability Zone. AgentCore shares ENIs across agents that use the same subnet and security group configuration. An interface you find might therefore also serve other agents.

To assess and track multi-AZ posture at scale, use AWS Resilience Hub. Include your harness's application resources in a Resilience Hub application and run a resiliency assessment. The assessment can flag single-AZ concentration against your resiliency policy. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is not among the services on the Resilience Hub list of supported resources. An assessment might therefore evaluate only the supported resources your harness depends on, such as Amazon EFS file systems, NAT gateways, and databases. Continue to verify your harness's own subnet placement directly.

- [Subnets for your VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/configure-subnets.html)
- [DescribeSubnets (Amazon EC2 API Reference)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/APIReference/API_DescribeSubnets.html)
- [What is AWS Resilience Hub?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/resilience-hub/latest/userguide/what-is.html)

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Harness.5](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlharness5)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Harness.5](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlharness5)): This implementation guidance recommends supplying two or more subnets from different Availability Zones in `$.environment.agentCoreRuntimeEnvironment.networkConfiguration.networkModeConfig.subnets[*]`, the subnets in your harness's VPC network configuration. Spreading the elastic network interfaces that AgentCore creates for your harness across zones helps its VPC connectivity survive the loss of a single Availability Zone.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Harness.17

*Guidance — Directive*

Configure the security groups that govern your harness's network traffic following least-privilege best practices. In VPC network mode, AgentCore attaches the groups in `$.environment.agentCoreRuntimeEnvironment.networkConfiguration.networkModeConfig.securityGroups[*]` to the elastic network interfaces it creates in your subnets for harness sessions. These groups govern the traffic your sessions send to VPC resources, AWS service endpoints, and the internet. When your inbound JWT authorizer uses a managed private endpoint, the groups in `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]` attach to its VPC Lattice resource gateway. That resource gateway carries authorizer traffic to your private identity provider.

Restrict both inbound and outbound rules to only the required sources and destinations (IP address ranges, referenced security groups, or prefix lists), protocols, and ports. Harness sessions run on a managed AgentCore Runtime that initiates outbound connections. The session groups generally need no inbound rules. Replace the default outbound rule that allows all traffic with rules for the destinations your harness uses. For example, allow HTTPS to the security groups of your Amazon ECR and Amazon Bedrock runtime interface endpoints. Allow HTTPS to the Amazon S3 prefix list for your gateway endpoint. Allow only your database port, such as TCP 3306, to a database's security group. Allow only TCP 2049 to the security groups of file system mount targets. Limit internet egress for Git skills, remote MCP servers, or public container image pulls to the required ports and, where known, address ranges. Where the peer is an AWS resource in a security group, reference that security group instead of its address range. The rule then follows the peer's network interfaces rather than addresses that can change. For the authorizer's resource gateway, allow outbound traffic only to your identity provider endpoint on the protocol and port it listens on. If you omit those groups, the default security group for the VPC is used. Specify dedicated groups instead. Avoid rules that permit 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0, particularly on administrative or sensitive ports. Rule changes apply automatically to every resource that uses a group. Review the groups themselves, not only the harness configuration.

To govern security groups at scale, use AWS Firewall Manager security group policies across your organization in AWS Organizations. You can scope each policy by account, organizational unit (OU), or tag. A common policy applies a baseline security group. A content audit policy audits inbound and outbound rules against an allow list or block list. It flags noncompliant groups in a central dashboard, can notify you, and can remediate them automatically. A usage audit policy identifies unused or redundant groups and can remove or consolidate them. To focus a content audit policy, tag the security groups your harnesses use and scope the policy to that tag. AgentCore creates and manages harness network interfaces through a service-linked role. Firewall Manager can't update security groups on requester-managed network interfaces. Confirm how a common policy treats these interfaces before you rely on it. A usage audit policy may treat a group that your harness configuration references as unused when no network interface currently uses it. Review policy findings before you enable automatic remediation.

To verify unintended access permitted by your security groups, use Amazon VPC Network Access Analyzer. Define a Network Access Scope for the access you consider unintended. For example, match any path that reaches administrative ports 22 or 3389 from an unrestricted address. You can also match paths from your harness security groups to an internet gateway and exclude the ports you require. Create the scope with `CreateNetworkInsightsAccessScope`, run it with `StartNetworkInsightsAccessScopeAnalysis`, and review the findings. Network Access Analyzer reasons about the security group together with the route table, network ACL, and public IP assignment. This helps you identify unintended network access relative to your security and compliance requirements.

- [Using content audit security group policies with Firewall Manager](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/security-group-policies-audit.html)
- [How to continuously audit and limit security groups with AWS Firewall Manager](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/how-to-continuously-audit-and-limit-security-groups-with-aws-firewall-manager/)
- [What is Network Access Analyzer?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/network-access-analyzer/what-is-network-access-analyzer.html)

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Harness.8](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlharness8)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Harness.8](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlharness8)): This implementation guidance recommends restricting the inbound and outbound rules on your harness's security groups to the required addresses, protocols, and ports. Excluding unrestricted addresses such as 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 from those inbound and outbound rules helps reduce the network exposure of your harness.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Memory.1

*CloudFormation hook — Proactive*

Validates template properties before provisioning.

- `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Memory`: `$.MemoryExecutionRoleArn`

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Memory.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlmemory1)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Memory.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlmemory1)): This implementation guidance recommends validating the trust policy of `$.MemoryExecutionRoleArn`, your memory's execution role, including source conditions on service principals, before provisioning. This helps prevent the memory from being provisioned when that trust policy can grant public access, or role assumption beyond the reference policy you maintain.

**Reference:** This implementation recommends using IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks.

Custom policy checks (`CheckNoPublicAccess`, `CheckNoNewAccess`) use automated reasoning to provide a higher level of assurance. They provably verify that a policy does not grant public access or grant new access beyond a reference policy you maintain.

The first reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` allowlists the principals this role's trust policy may grant assumption to. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption beyond that allowlist. Example reference policies for role trust policies are available in the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples repository.

The second reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` encodes the source conditions you accept when the service principal assumes the role: one sts:AssumeRole statement per accepted combination of the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, with placeholders for your account, organization, and resource values. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption that no statement of the reference allows, including grants that omit the condition keys or weaken them with `IfExists`.
- [IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access-analyzer-custom-policy-checks.html)
- [IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples](https://github.com/aws-samples/iam-access-analyzer-custom-policy-check-samples)

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Memory.2

A periodic rule that evaluates via the API operation chain below.

1. Call `bedrock-agentcore-control:ListMemories`; check `$.memories[*].id`
2. Call `bedrock-agentcore-control:GetMemory` with `$.memoryId`; check `$.memory.memoryExecutionRoleArn`
3. Call `iam:GetRole` with `$.RoleName`; check `$.Role.AssumeRolePolicyDocument`
4. Call `accessanalyzer:CheckNoPublicAccess` with `$.policyDocument`, `$.resourceType` = `AWS::IAM::AssumeRolePolicyDocument`; check `$.result`
5. Call `accessanalyzer:CheckNoNewAccess` with `$.newPolicyDocument`, `$.existingPolicyDocument`, `$.policyType` = `RESOURCE_POLICY`; check `$.result`
6. Call `accessanalyzer:CheckNoNewAccess` with `$.newPolicyDocument`, `$.existingPolicyDocument`, `$.policyType` = `RESOURCE_POLICY`; check `$.result`

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Memory.3

*IAM role trust policy — Preventive*

Governs the IAM role trust policy statements below (the role is the resource).

| Principal | Actions | Condition keys |
|---|---|---|
| `bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com` | `sts:AssumeRole` | `aws:SourceAccount` (alternatives: `aws:SourceOrgID`, `aws:SourceOrgPaths`), `aws:SourceArn` |

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Memory.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlmemory1)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Memory.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlmemory1)): This implementation guidance recommends a trust policy that restricts assumption of your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory's IAM execution role, `$.memoryExecutionRoleArn`, to the `bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com` service principal with the `aws:SourceArn` and `aws:SourceAccount` condition keys. These conditions help prevent Amazon Bedrock AgentCore from assuming the role on behalf of memory resources outside the sources you specify.

**Reference:** Confirm that IAM role trust policies grant access only to the AWS service principals you intend. Review the `Principal` element of each policy and verify it names only the service principals your workload requires.

As a defense-in-depth measure, use the `aws:SourceOrgID`, `aws:SourceOrgPaths`, `aws:SourceAccount`, or `aws:SourceArn` condition keys. These scope access performed on behalf of resources within a particular organization, specific organizational units, a specific AWS account, or a particular resource, respectively. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Memory.4

*Resource control policy (RCP) — Preventive*

Governs the IAM permissions below.

| Actions | Resources | Condition keys |
|---|---|---|
| `sts:AssumeRole` | `*` | `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`, `aws:PrincipalOrgID` (alternatives: `aws:PrincipalAccount`, `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`) |

These conditions help prevent principals outside your organization from assuming your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory's execution role, `$.memoryExecutionRoleArn`.

**Reference:** To restrict access to trusted identities, use the `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`, or `aws:PrincipalAccount` condition keys. These scope access to IAM principals within a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. These keys do not contain your organization or account values for requests by AWS service principals, so apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `false`. As a defense-in-depth measure, use the `aws:SourceOrgID`, `aws:SourceOrgPaths`, `aws:SourceAccount`, or `aws:SourceArn` condition keys to restrict service access to your roles. These scope access performed on behalf of resources within a particular organization, specific organizational units, a specific AWS account, or a particular resource, respectively. Apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `true`. Also require that `aws:SourceAccount` is present in the request context, because not every service integration populates these keys. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Memory.7

Flagging Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memories whose key is not a customer managed key in your account, or whose key material is imported or held in an external key store, helps you detect where you do not control the key policy, lifecycle, or key material.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Oauth2CredentialProvider.1

*Guidance — Directive*

When you configure a managed private endpoint on an OAuth2 credential provider, supply two or more subnets that resolve to different Availability Zones. Private endpoints are configured in the custom provider configuration (`customOauth2ProviderConfig`). Set the subnets in `privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds` when you call `CreateOauth2CredentialProvider` or `UpdateOauth2CredentialProvider`. Apply the same rule to each `privateEndpointOverrides` entry that uses a managed VPC resource. AgentCore Identity places its managed VPC Lattice resource gateway in these subnets. The gateway's elastic network interfaces (ENIs) carry traffic to your VPC-hosted identity provider. Placing those interfaces in more than one Availability Zone helps that connectivity survive the loss of a single zone.

Subnet-to-AZ membership is a property of each subnet, not of the credential provider. Before you supply subnet IDs, call Amazon EC2 `DescribeSubnets` and use the `AvailabilityZone` response field to confirm that they belong to distinct Availability Zones. Each subnet also needs network access to your identity provider's discovery and token endpoints. Standardize on infrastructure-as-code review so that the templates and modules that create `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::OAuth2CredentialProvider` resources supply at least two subnets from different Availability Zones.

To verify the deployed state, call `GetOauth2CredentialProvider` and review the subnet IDs returned in the custom provider's private endpoint configuration. Then enumerate the resource gateway's network interfaces with Amazon EC2 `DescribeNetworkInterfaces` and confirm that their subnets span more than one Availability Zone. The managed resource gateway is read-only to you. To change its zones, update the subnet list on the credential provider. `UpdateOauth2CredentialProvider` requires the vendor and the full provider configuration.

To assess and track multi-AZ posture at scale, use AWS Resilience Hub. Include your application's resources in a Resilience Hub application and run a resiliency assessment, which can flag single-AZ concentration against your resiliency policy. The list of resources that Resilience Hub supports does not include Amazon Bedrock AgentCore or Amazon VPC Lattice. Use it for the supported resources in your application, such as those that host your identity provider, alongside the subnet and network interface checks above.

- [Subnets for your VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/configure-subnets.html)
- [DescribeSubnets (Amazon EC2 API Reference)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/APIReference/API_DescribeSubnets.html)
- [What is AWS Resilience Hub?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/resilience-hub/latest/userguide/what-is.html)

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Oauth2CredentialProvider.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controloauth2credentialprovider1)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Oauth2CredentialProvider.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controloauth2credentialprovider1)): This implementation guidance recommends supplying two or more subnets from different Availability Zones in `$.oauth2ProviderConfigInput.customOauth2ProviderConfig.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds[*]`, the managed private endpoint subnets of your custom OAuth2 credential provider. Spreading the network interfaces of AgentCore Identity's managed VPC Lattice resource gateway across zones helps connectivity to your VPC-hosted identity provider survive the loss of a single Availability Zone.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Oauth2CredentialProvider.9

*Guidance — Directive*

Configure the security groups for your OAuth2 credential provider's private endpoint by following least-privilege best practices. These are the security groups that you list in `$.oauth2ProviderConfigInput.customOauth2ProviderConfig.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]` for a custom OAuth2 provider. They also include the groups in each per-domain `privateEndpointOverrides[*].privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]` entry. You set them when you call `CreateOauth2CredentialProvider` or `UpdateOauth2CredentialProvider`. AgentCore Identity associates them with the VPC Lattice resource gateway that it creates and manages in your subnets. Their outbound rules control the traffic that the resource gateway sends to your identity provider's discovery and token endpoints. If you specify no security groups, the default security group for the VPC is used. That group's default rules allow all outbound traffic and inbound traffic from resources assigned to the same group. Specify custom security groups for the private endpoint instead, and avoid rules that allow unrestricted traffic from or to 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0. Restrict both inbound and outbound rules to only the required sources and destinations (IP address ranges, referenced security groups, or prefix lists), protocols, and ports. For example, allow outbound HTTPS only on the port that your identity provider uses, typically 443, and only to its endpoints. Where the peer is an AWS resource in a security group, reference that security group instead of its address range. The rule then follows the peer's network interfaces rather than addresses that can change.

To govern security groups at scale, use AWS Firewall Manager security group policies across your organization in AWS Organizations. You can scope these policies by account, organizational unit (OU), or tag. A common security group policy applies a baseline security group to in-scope resources. A content audit security group policy audits inbound and outbound rules against an allow list or a block list. It flags noncompliant security groups in a central dashboard, sends notifications, and can automatically remediate noncompliant rules. A usage audit security group policy can remove unused or redundant security groups.

To verify unintended access that your security groups permit, use Amazon VPC Network Access Analyzer. Define a Network Access Scope for the access that you consider unintended. For example, the scope might match any path that reaches administrative ports 22 or 3389 from an unrestricted address. Create the scope with `CreateNetworkInsightsAccessScope`, run an analysis with `StartNetworkInsightsAccessScopeAnalysis`, and review the findings. Network Access Analyzer evaluates the security group together with the route table, network ACL, and public IP address assignment. This helps you identify unintended network access relative to your security and compliance requirements.

- [Using content audit security group policies with Firewall Manager](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/security-group-policies-audit.html)
- [How to continuously audit and limit security groups with AWS Firewall Manager](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/how-to-continuously-audit-and-limit-security-groups-with-aws-firewall-manager/)
- [What is Network Access Analyzer?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/network-access-analyzer/what-is-network-access-analyzer.html)

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.OnlineEvaluationConfig.4

*CloudFormation hook — Proactive*

Validates template properties before provisioning.

- `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::OnlineEvaluationConfig`: `$.EvaluationExecutionRoleArn`

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.OnlineEvaluationConfig.2](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlonlineevaluationconfig2)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.OnlineEvaluationConfig.2](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlonlineevaluationconfig2)): This implementation guidance recommends validating the trust policy of `$.EvaluationExecutionRoleArn`, your online evaluation config's execution role, including source conditions on service principals, before provisioning. This helps prevent the online evaluation config from being provisioned when that trust policy can grant public access, or role assumption beyond the reference policy you maintain.

**Reference:** This implementation recommends using IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks. Custom policy checks (`CheckNoPublicAccess`, `CheckNoNewAccess`) use automated reasoning to provide a higher level of assurance. They provably verify that a policy does not grant public access or grant new access beyond a reference policy you maintain. The first reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` allowlists the principals this role's trust policy may grant assumption to. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption beyond that allowlist. Example reference policies for role trust policies are available in the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples repository. The second reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` encodes the source conditions you accept when the service principal assumes the role: one role-assumption statement per accepted combination of the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, with placeholders for your account, organization, and resource values. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption that no statement of the reference allows, including grants that omit the condition keys or weaken them with `IfExists`.
- [IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access-analyzer-custom-policy-checks.html)
- [IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples](https://github.com/aws-samples/iam-access-analyzer-custom-policy-check-samples)

3. Call `iam:GetRole` with `$.RoleName`; check `$.Role.AssumeRolePolicyDocument`
4. Call `accessanalyzer:CheckNoPublicAccess` with `$.policyDocument`, `$.resourceType` = `AWS::IAM::AssumeRolePolicyDocument`; check `$.result`
5. Call `accessanalyzer:CheckNoNewAccess` with `$.newPolicyDocument`, `$.existingPolicyDocument`, `$.policyType` = `RESOURCE_POLICY`; check `$.result`
6. Call `accessanalyzer:CheckNoNewAccess` with `$.newPolicyDocument`, `$.existingPolicyDocument`, `$.policyType` = `RESOURCE_POLICY`; check `$.result`

These conditions help prevent AgentCore from assuming the role on behalf of online evaluation configs and evaluators outside the sources you specify.

**Reference:** Confirm that IAM role trust policies grant access only to the AWS service principals you intend. Review the `Principal` element of each policy and verify it names only the service principals your workload requires.

As a defense-in-depth measure, use the `aws:SourceOrgID`, `aws:SourceOrgPaths`, `aws:SourceAccount`, or `aws:SourceArn` condition keys. These scope access performed on behalf of resources within a particular organization, specific organizational units, a specific AWS account, or a particular resource, respectively. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.
