**Reference:** To restrict access to trusted identities, use the `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`, or `aws:PrincipalAccount` condition keys. These scope access to IAM principals within a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. These keys do not contain your organization or account values for requests by AWS service principals, so apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `false`. As a defense-in-depth measure, use the `aws:SourceOrgID`, `aws:SourceOrgPaths`, `aws:SourceAccount`, or `aws:SourceArn` condition keys to restrict service access to your roles. These scope access performed on behalf of resources within a particular organization, specific organizational units, a specific AWS account, or a particular resource, respectively. Apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `true`. Also require that `aws:SourceAccount` is present in the request context, because not every service integration populates these keys. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.PaymentManager.1

*CloudFormation hook — Proactive*

Validates template properties before provisioning.

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.PaymentManager.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlpaymentmanager1)): This implementation guidance recommends validating the trust policy of `$.RoleArn`, your payment manager's service role, including source conditions on service principals, before provisioning. This helps prevent the payment manager from being provisioned when that trust policy can grant public access, or role assumption beyond the reference policy you maintain.

**Reference:** This implementation recommends using IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks. Custom policy checks (`CheckNoPublicAccess`, `CheckNoNewAccess`) use automated reasoning to provide a higher level of assurance. They provably verify that a policy does not grant public access or grant new access beyond a reference policy you maintain. The first reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` allowlists the principals this role's trust policy may grant assumption to. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption beyond that allowlist. Example reference policies for role trust policies are available in the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples repository. The second reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` encodes the source conditions you accept when the service principal assumes the role: one role-assumption statement per accepted combination of the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, with placeholders for your account, organization, and resource values. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption that no statement of the reference allows, including grants that omit the condition keys or weaken them with `IfExists`.
- [IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access-analyzer-custom-policy-checks.html)
- [IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples](https://github.com/aws-samples/iam-access-analyzer-custom-policy-check-samples)

**Reference:** To restrict access to trusted identities, use the `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`, or `aws:PrincipalAccount` condition keys. These scope access to IAM principals within a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. These keys do not contain your organization or account values for requests by AWS service principals, so apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `false`. As a defense-in-depth measure, use the `aws:SourceOrgID`, `aws:SourceOrgPaths`, `aws:SourceAccount`, or `aws:SourceArn` condition keys to restrict service access to your roles. These scope access performed on behalf of resources within a particular organization, specific organizational units, a specific AWS account, or a particular resource, respectively. Apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `true`. Also require that `aws:SourceAccount` is present in the request context, because not every service integration populates these keys. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.PaymentManager.8

*Guidance — Directive*

When your payment manager uses a custom JSON Web Token (JWT) authorizer with a managed private endpoint, supply two or more subnets from different Availability Zones (AZs). Set them in `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds[*]` when you call `CreatePaymentManager` or `UpdatePaymentManager`. AgentCore creates and manages a VPC Lattice resource gateway for your private identity provider and places it in those subnets. The resource gateway is built from elastic network interfaces (ENIs) in the listed subnets, so the subnets' AZs decide where those ENIs reside. Spreading the ENIs across AZs helps AgentCore keep reaching your identity provider's discovery and JSON Web Key Set (JWKS) endpoints if a single AZ is lost. Choose only subnets that can reach those endpoints.

Subnet-to-AZ membership is a property of each subnet, not of the payment manager. Before you supply subnet IDs, call the Amazon EC2 `DescribeSubnets` operation. Confirm that the `AvailabilityZone` field differs across the chosen subnets. Standardize on infrastructure-as-code review so that the templates, modules, and scripts that create or update payment managers supply at least two subnets from different AZs. The AWS CloudFormation resource type for payment managers does not currently list private endpoint properties. Include your SDK and AWS CLI automation in that review.

To verify the deployed state, call `GetPaymentManager` and read back the subnet IDs in the returned authorizer configuration. Then call `DescribeNetworkInterfaces` filtered on your VPC. Find the requester-managed interfaces whose description names a resource gateway. Confirm that the subnets of those interfaces span more than one AZ.

To assess and track multi-AZ posture at scale, use AWS Resilience Hub. Include the application resources around your payment manager in a Resilience Hub application, such as the compute and load balancers that host your private identity provider. Then run a resiliency assessment, which flags single-AZ concentration against your resiliency policy. Resilience Hub assesses only the resource types it supports. Its supported resources do not list Amazon Bedrock AgentCore or Amazon VPC Lattice. Keep the network interface check as your direct verification of the resource gateway placement.

- [Subnets for your VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/configure-subnets.html)
- [DescribeSubnets (Amazon EC2 API Reference)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/APIReference/API_DescribeSubnets.html)
- [What is AWS Resilience Hub?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/resilience-hub/latest/userguide/what-is.html)

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.PaymentManager.4](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlpaymentmanager4)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.PaymentManager.4](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlpaymentmanager4)): This implementation guidance recommends supplying two or more subnets from different Availability Zones in `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds[*]`, the subnets for your payment manager's managed private endpoint. Spreading the elastic network interfaces of the VPC Lattice resource gateway that AgentCore creates for your payment manager across zones helps AgentCore's private connectivity to your identity provider survive the loss of a single Availability Zone.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.PaymentManager.15

*Guidance — Directive*

Apply least-privilege rules to the security groups for your payment manager's managed private endpoint. You can name up to five groups in `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]` when you call `CreatePaymentManager` or `UpdatePaymentManager`. AgentCore attaches them to the VPC Lattice resource gateway it creates in your VPC to reach your private identity provider's OIDC discovery and JWKS endpoints. Their rules control the traffic that the gateway's network interfaces send to your identity provider. If you don't name any groups, the VPC's default security group is used, so review its rules as well. Restrict both inbound and outbound rules to only the sources and destinations you need (IP address ranges, referenced security groups, or prefix lists), protocols, and ports, such as HTTPS to your identity provider's endpoints. Don't allow unrestricted access from or to any IP address (0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0). If the peer is an AWS resource in a security group, such as an internal Application Load Balancer in front of your identity provider, reference that security group instead of its address range. The rule then follows the peer's network interfaces rather than addresses that can change.

To govern security groups at scale, use AWS Firewall Manager security group policies across your organization in AWS Organizations, scoped by account, organizational unit (OU), or tag. A common security group policy applies a baseline security group. A content audit security group policy audits inbound and outbound rules against an allow list or block list. It flags noncompliant groups in a central dashboard, sends notifications, and can remediate them automatically. You can include the Amazon VPC security group resource type in a content audit policy's scope, which brings the groups you name for the private endpoint into scope directly. A usage audit security group policy removes unused or redundant security groups.

To check for unintended access that your security groups allow, use Amazon VPC Network Access Analyzer. Define a Network Access Scope (`CreateNetworkInsightsAccessScope`) for the access that you consider unintended, for example any path that reaches administrative ports 22 or 3389 from an unrestricted address. Then run an analysis (`StartNetworkInsightsAccessScopeAnalysis`) and review the findings. Network Access Analyzer evaluates the security group together with the route table, network ACL, and public IP assignment to find network access that doesn't match your security and compliance requirements.

- [Using content audit security group policies with Firewall Manager](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/security-group-policies-audit.html)
- [How to continuously audit and limit security groups with AWS Firewall Manager](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/how-to-continuously-audit-and-limit-security-groups-with-aws-firewall-manager/)
- [What is Network Access Analyzer?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/network-access-analyzer/what-is-network-access-analyzer.html)

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.PaymentManager.7](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlpaymentmanager7)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.PaymentManager.7](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlpaymentmanager7)): This implementation guidance recommends restricting the inbound and outbound rules on the security groups in `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]`, the groups associated with your payment manager's managed VPC Lattice resource gateway, to the required addresses, protocols, and ports. Excluding unrestricted addresses such as 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 from those inbound and outbound rules helps reduce the network exposure of the resource gateway's network interfaces.

2. Call `bedrock-agentcore-control:GetPaymentManager` with `$.paymentManagerId`; check `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]`, `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.vpcIdentifier`

Call `ec2:DescribeSecurityGroups` with `$.GroupId[*]`, `$.Filter[*].Name`, `$.Filter[*].Value[*]`; check `$.securityGroupInfo[*].ipPermissions[*].ipProtocol` = `-1`, `$.securityGroupInfo[*].ipPermissions[*].fromPort`, `$.securityGroupInfo[*].ipPermissions[*].toPort`, `$.securityGroupInfo[*].ipPermissions[*].ipRanges[*].cidrIp` = `0.0.0.0/0`, `$.securityGroupInfo[*].ipPermissions[*].ipv6Ranges[*].cidrIpv6` = `::/0`, `$.securityGroupInfo[*].ipPermissions[*].groups[*].groupId`, `$.securityGroupInfo[*].ipPermissions[*].prefixListIds[*].prefixListId`, `$.securityGroupInfo[*].ipPermissionsEgress[*].ipProtocol` = `-1`, `$.securityGroupInfo[*].ipPermissionsEgress[*].fromPort`, `$.securityGroupInfo[*].ipPermissionsEgress[*].toPort`, `$.securityGroupInfo[*].ipPermissionsEgress[*].ipRanges[*].cidrIp` = `0.0.0.0/0`, `$.securityGroupInfo[*].ipPermissionsEgress[*].ipv6Ranges[*].cidrIpv6` = `::/0`, `$.securityGroupInfo[*].ipPermissionsEgress[*].groups[*].groupId`, `$.securityGroupInfo[*].ipPermissionsEgress[*].prefixListIds[*].prefixListId`
4. Call `ec2:GetManagedPrefixListEntries` with `$.PrefixListId`; check `$.entrySet[*].cidr` = `0.0.0.0/0`, `$.entrySet[*].cidr` = `::/0`

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Registry.2

*Guidance — Directive*

When your registry uses the `CUSTOM_JWT` authorizer with a managed private endpoint to reach an identity provider hosted in your VPC, supply two or more subnets that resolve to different Availability Zones. Set these subnets in `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds[*]` when you call `CreateRegistry`, or in `$.authorizerConfiguration.optionalValue.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds[*]` when you call `UpdateRegistry`. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore places the network interfaces of the VPC Lattice resource gateway that it manages on your behalf in the subnets that you list. Spreading those subnets across zones places network interfaces in more than one Availability Zone. This helps your registry's private connectivity to the identity provider's OIDC discovery and JWKS endpoints survive the loss of a single zone. Choose only subnets from which those identity provider endpoints are reachable. Changing the authorizer configuration can disrupt existing consumers of a registry, so plan subnet changes on a registry that is in use.

Subnet-to-Availability Zone membership is a property of each subnet, not of the registry. Before you supply subnet IDs, use the Amazon EC2 `DescribeSubnets` operation to confirm from the `AvailabilityZone` field that the chosen subnets belong to distinct Availability Zones. Standardize on infrastructure-as-code and automation review so that the templates, modules, and scripts that call `CreateRegistry` or `UpdateRegistry` supply at least two subnets from different Availability Zones.

To verify the deployed state, call `GetRegistry` and review the managed private endpoint subnet IDs in the returned authorizer configuration. Then use the Amazon EC2 `DescribeNetworkInterfaces` operation to enumerate the network interfaces in those subnets. Confirm that the resource gateway's network interfaces span more than one Availability Zone.

To assess and track multi-AZ posture at scale, include the application resources around your registry, such as the resources that host your identity provider, in an AWS Resilience Hub application. Then run a resiliency assessment, which flags single-AZ concentration against your resiliency policy. Resilience Hub assesses only the resource types that it supports, so confirm which of your resources it can assess.

- [Subnets for your VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/configure-subnets.html)
- [DescribeSubnets (Amazon EC2 API Reference)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/APIReference/API_DescribeSubnets.html)
- [What is AWS Resilience Hub?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/resilience-hub/latest/userguide/what-is.html)

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Registry.2](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlregistry2)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Registry.2](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlregistry2)): This implementation guidance recommends supplying two or more subnets from different Availability Zones in `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.subnetIds[*]`, the subnet IDs of your registry's managed private endpoint. Spreading the network interfaces of the AgentCore-managed VPC Lattice resource gateway across zones helps private connectivity to your identity provider survive the loss of a single Availability Zone.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Registry.5

*Guidance — Directive*

If your registry's custom JWT authorizer uses a managed private endpoint, AgentCore creates and manages a VPC Lattice resource gateway in your VPC. Its network interfaces carry the registry's traffic to your identity provider's discovery and JWKS endpoints. You associate security groups with it through `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]` on `CreateRegistry`, or its `optionalValue` counterpart on `UpdateRegistry`. If you don't specify any, the VPC's default security group is associated.

Configure these security groups following least-privilege best practices. Restrict inbound and outbound rules to only the required sources and destinations (IP address ranges, referenced security groups, or prefix lists), protocols, and ports. Outbound rules on a resource gateway's security groups control its traffic to your identity provider. Your identity provider typically uses port 443 for HTTPS. Where the peer is an AWS resource in a security group, reference that security group instead of its address range. For example, reference your identity provider's security group in the resource gateway's outbound rules. The rule then follows the peer's network interfaces rather than addresses that can change.

To govern security groups at scale, use AWS Firewall Manager security group policies across your organization in AWS Organizations. You can scope these policies by account, organizational unit (OU), or tag. A common security group policy applies a baseline security group. A content audit security group policy audits inbound and outbound rules against an allow list or a block list. It flags noncompliant security groups in a central dashboard, sends notifications, and can automatically remediate noncompliant rules. A usage audit security group policy removes unused or redundant security groups. Content audit policies can scope Amazon VPC security groups directly. That scope includes the security groups you create and associate with the AgentCore-managed resource gateway.

To verify unintended access that your security groups permit, use Amazon VPC Network Access Analyzer. Define a Network Access Scope for the access you consider unintended. For example, match any path that reaches administrative ports 22 or 3389 from an unrestricted address. Create the scope by calling `CreateNetworkInsightsAccessScope`, then run an analysis by calling `StartNetworkInsightsAccessScopeAnalysis` and review the findings. Network Access Analyzer evaluates your security groups together with route tables, network ACLs, and public IP assignments. This helps you identify unintended network access relative to your security and compliance requirements.

- [Using content audit security group policies with Firewall Manager](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/security-group-policies-audit.html)
- [How to continuously audit and limit security groups with AWS Firewall Manager](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/how-to-continuously-audit-and-limit-security-groups-with-aws-firewall-manager/)
- [What is Network Access Analyzer?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/network-access-analyzer/what-is-network-access-analyzer.html)

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Registry.4](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlregistry4)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.Registry.4](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlregistry4)): This implementation guidance recommends restricting the inbound and outbound rules on the security groups in `$.authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer.privateEndpoint.managedVpcResource.securityGroupIds[*]` to the required addresses, protocols, and ports. Excluding unrestricted addresses such as 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 from those inbound and outbound rules helps reduce the network exposure of your registry's private endpoint.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.RegistryRecord.1

*AWS Config rule — Detective*

A periodic rule that evaluates via the API operation chain below.

1. Call `bedrock-agentcore-control:ListRegistries`; check `$.registries[*].registryId`
2. Call `bedrock-agentcore-control:ListRegistryRecords` with `$.registryId`; check `$.registryRecords[*].recordId`
3. Call `bedrock-agentcore-control:GetRegistryRecord` with `$.registryId`, `$.recordId`; check `$.synchronizationConfiguration.fromUrl.credentialProviderConfigurations[*].credentialProvider.iamCredentialProvider.roleArn`
4. Call `iam:GetRole` with `$.RoleName`; check `$.Role.AssumeRolePolicyDocument`
5. Call `accessanalyzer:CheckNoPublicAccess` with `$.policyDocument`, `$.resourceType` = `AWS::IAM::AssumeRolePolicyDocument`; check `$.result`
6. Call `accessanalyzer:CheckNoNewAccess` with `$.newPolicyDocument`, `$.existingPolicyDocument`, `$.policyType` = `RESOURCE_POLICY`; check `$.result`
7. Call `accessanalyzer:CheckNoNewAccess` with `$.newPolicyDocument`, `$.existingPolicyDocument`, `$.policyType` = `RESOURCE_POLICY`; check `$.result`

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.RegistryRecord.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlregistryrecord1)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.RegistryRecord.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlregistryrecord1)): This implementation guidance recommends reading `$.synchronizationConfiguration.fromUrl.credentialProviderConfigurations[*].credentialProvider.iamCredentialProvider.roleArn`, your registry record's sync role, then evaluating `$.Role.AssumeRolePolicyDocument`, that role's trust policy, with IAM Access Analyzer. Flagging trust policies that allow public role assumption, or assumption beyond your reference policy, or that omit the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, helps you detect overly permissive role assumption.

**Reference:** This implementation recommends using IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks. Custom policy checks (`CheckNoPublicAccess`, `CheckNoNewAccess`) use automated reasoning to provide a higher level of assurance. They provably verify that a policy does not grant public access or grant new access beyond a reference policy you maintain. The first reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` allowlists the principals this role's trust policy may grant assumption to. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption beyond that allowlist. Example reference policies for role trust policies are available in the IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples repository. The second reference policy for `CheckNoNewAccess` encodes the source conditions you accept when the service principal assumes the role: one role-assumption statement per accepted combination of the `aws:SourceArn`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID`, or `aws:SourceOrgPaths` condition keys, with placeholders for your account, organization, and resource values. The check fails when the trust policy grants role assumption that no statement of the reference allows, including grants that omit the condition keys or weaken them with `IfExists`.
- [IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access-analyzer-custom-policy-checks.html)
- [IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks samples](https://github.com/aws-samples/iam-access-analyzer-custom-policy-check-samples)

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.RegistryRecord.3

*Resource control policy (RCP) — Preventive*

Governs the IAM permissions below.

| Actions | Resources | Condition keys |
|---|---|---|
| `sts:AssumeRole` | `*` | `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`, `aws:PrincipalOrgID` (alternatives: `aws:PrincipalAccount`, `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`) |
| `sts:AssumeRole` | `*` | `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`, `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID` (alternatives: `aws:SourceOrgPaths`) |

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.RegistryRecord.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlregistryrecord1)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.RegistryRecord.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlregistryrecord1)): This implementation guidance recommends restricting `sts:AssumeRole` with the `aws:PrincipalOrgID` condition key in a resource control policy (RCP), while exempting AWS services acting on your behalf (`aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`) and scoping those service requests with `aws:SourceOrgID`. These conditions help prevent principals outside your organization from assuming your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore registry record's sync role, `$.synchronizationConfiguration.fromUrl.credentialProviderConfigurations[*].credentialProvider.iamCredentialProvider.roleArn` and `$.synchronizationConfiguration.optionalValue.fromUrl.credentialProviderConfigurations[*].credentialProvider.iamCredentialProvider.roleArn`.

**Reference:** To restrict access to trusted identities, use the `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths`, or `aws:PrincipalAccount` condition keys. These scope access to IAM principals within a particular organization, specific organizational units, or a specific AWS account, respectively. These keys do not contain your organization or account values for requests by AWS service principals, so apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `false`. As a defense-in-depth measure, use the `aws:SourceOrgID`, `aws:SourceOrgPaths`, `aws:SourceAccount`, or `aws:SourceArn` condition keys to restrict service access to your roles. These scope access performed on behalf of resources within a particular organization, specific organizational units, a specific AWS account, or a particular resource, respectively. Apply them only when `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `true`. Also require that `aws:SourceAccount` is present in the request context, because not every service integration populates these keys. Choose the condition key that matches the granularity of the restriction you want to enforce.

- [RCP sample: identity perimeter policy](https://github.com/aws-samples/data-perimeter-policy-examples/blob/main/resource_control_policies/identity_perimeter_rcp.json)

| `bedrock-agentcore:UntagResource` | `arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:*:*:token-vault/*` | `aws:TagKeys` |

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.TokenVault.2](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controltokenvault2)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.TokenVault.2](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controltokenvault2)): This implementation guidance recommends restricting `bedrock-agentcore:TagResource` with the `aws:RequestTag/owner`, `aws:RequestTag/purpose`, and `aws:TagKeys` condition keys in a service control policy (SCP). These conditions help prevent tagging an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore token vault without the owner and purpose tag keys, or removing them through `bedrock-agentcore:UntagResource`.

**Reference:** Use `aws:RequestTag/owner` and `aws:RequestTag/purpose` so that a request omitting either one is denied. Use `aws:TagKeys` to require each key in its exact case because the tag-key portion of `aws:RequestTag/tag-key` is not case-sensitive. Also use `aws:TagKeys` on the untag action so that a request removing either key is denied.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.WorkloadIdentity.1

*CloudFormation hook — Proactive*

Validates template properties before provisioning.

- `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::WorkloadIdentity`: `$.Tags[*].Key`, `$.Tags[*].Value`

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.WorkloadIdentity.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlworkloadidentity1)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.WorkloadIdentity.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlworkloadidentity1)): This implementation guidance recommends validating, before provisioning, that `$.Tags[*].Key` and `$.Tags[*].Value` declare owner and purpose tags. Requiring those tags helps prevent an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore workload identity that omits them from being provisioned and helps keep ownership and business function attributable.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.WorkloadIdentity.2

*AWS Config rule — Detective*

A change-triggered rule that evaluates configuration item properties on change.

- `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::WorkloadIdentity`: `$.tags[*].key`, `$.tags[*].value`

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.WorkloadIdentity.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlworkloadidentity1)): This implementation guidance recommends reading `$.tags[*].key` on each Amazon Bedrock AgentCore workload identity and flagging any that omit your required owner and purpose tag keys. Surfacing those resources helps you attribute each Amazon Bedrock AgentCore workload identity to an accountable owner and the business function it supports.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.WorkloadIdentity.3

*Service control policy (SCP) — Preventive*

Governs the IAM permissions below.

| Actions | Resources | Condition keys |
|---|---|---|
| `bedrock-agentcore:CreateWorkloadIdentity` | `*` | `aws:RequestTag/owner`, `aws:RequestTag/purpose`, `aws:TagKeys` |
| `bedrock-agentcore:TagResource` | `arn:*:bedrock-agentcore:*:*:workload-identity-directory/*/workload-identity/*` | `aws:RequestTag/owner`, `aws:RequestTag/purpose`, `aws:TagKeys` |

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.WorkloadIdentity.1](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlworkloadidentity1)

These conditions help prevent creating or tagging an AgentCore workload identity without the owner and purpose tag keys, or removing them through `bedrock-agentcore:UntagResource`.

**Reference:** Use `aws:RequestTag/owner` and `aws:RequestTag/purpose` so that a request omitting either one is denied. Use `aws:TagKeys` to require each key in its exact case because the tag-key portion of `aws:RequestTag/tag-key` is not case-sensitive. Also use `aws:TagKeys` on the untag action so that a request removing either key is denied.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.WorkloadIdentity.4

*CloudTrail management event — Detective*

Monitors the API calls below in CloudTrail.

- `cloudwatch-logs:DeleteDelivery` — `$.id`
- `cloudwatch-logs:DeleteDeliveryDestination` — `$.name`
- `cloudwatch-logs:DeleteDeliverySource` — `$.name`
- `cloudwatch-logs:DeleteLogGroup` — `$.logGroupName`
- `cloudwatch-logs:DeleteResourcePolicy` — `$.resourceArn`
- `cloudwatch-logs:PutDeliveryDestination` — `$.name`
- `cloudwatch-logs:PutDeliverySource` — `$.resourceArn`
- `cloudwatch-logs:PutResourcePolicy` — `$.resourceArn`
- `cloudwatch-logs:PutRetentionPolicy` — `$.logGroupName`
- `cloudwatch-logs:UpdateDeliveryConfiguration` — `$.id`

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.WorkloadIdentity.2](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlworkloadidentity2)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.WorkloadIdentity.2](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlworkloadidentity2)): This implementation guidance recommends recording the CloudWatch Logs operations that can disable or weaken the vended logs delivery for your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore workload identity. Recording calls such as `DeleteDelivery`, `DeleteDeliverySource`, and `PutRetentionPolicy`, together with the calling identity, helps you detect and attribute those changes.

### Implementation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.WorkloadIdentity.5

*AWS Config rule — Detective*

A periodic rule that evaluates via the API operation chain below.

1. Call `bedrock-agentcore-control:ListWorkloadIdentities`; check `$.workloadIdentities[*].workloadIdentityArn`
2. Call `cloudwatch-logs:DescribeDeliverySources` with `$.resourceArns[*]`; check `$.deliverySources[*].resourceArns[*]`, `$.deliverySources[*].logType` = `APPLICATION_LOGS`, `$.deliverySources[*].name`
3. Call `cloudwatch-logs:DescribeDeliveries` with `$.deliverySourceNames[*]`; check `$.deliveries[*].deliverySourceName`, `$.deliveries[*].deliveryDestinationType` = `CWL`, `$.deliveries[*].deliveryDestinationArn`

**Implements:** [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.WorkloadIdentity.2](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlworkloadidentity2)

**Scoping** (for [Mitigation.BEDROCK-AGENTCORE-CONTROL.WorkloadIdentity.2](#mitigationbedrock-agentcore-controlworkloadidentity2)): This implementation guidance recommends flagging an AgentCore workload identity with no vended logs delivery to CloudWatch Logs, read from `$.deliveries[*].deliveryDestinationType`, the delivery's destination type. Surfacing that gap helps you detect AgentCore Identity operation activity that is not being recorded for review.

## Appendix

### Resources

#### AgentRuntime

*COMPUTE_RESOURCE*

An agent runtime is a managed hosting environment for an AI agent or tool built with any framework or foundation model. You package your code as a container image or code bundle. The service runs it on demand and handles scaling and infrastructure management.

- IAM resource ARN: `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:runtime/${RuntimeId}`
- CloudFormation: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Runtime`, `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::ResourcePolicy`
- AWS Config: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Runtime`
- 12 operations, 15 threats, 13 mitigations

#### AgentRuntimeEndpoint

*AI_RESOURCE*

An agent runtime endpoint is a named, stable access point that routes invocations to a specific version of an AgentCore Runtime. Each runtime receives a default endpoint that automatically follows the newest version. You can add named endpoints for environments such as development, staging, and production.

- IAM resource ARN: `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:runtime/${RuntimeId}/runtime-endpoint/${Name}`
- CloudFormation: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::RuntimeEndpoint`, `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::ResourcePolicy`
- AWS Config: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::RuntimeEndpoint`
- 11 operations, 5 threats, 5 mitigations

#### ApiKeyCredentialProvider

*CRYPTOGRAPHIC_MATERIAL*

An API key credential provider stores an API key that your AI agents use to authenticate with external services and third-party APIs. It helps keep sensitive keys out of agent code, prompts, and configuration files.

- IAM resource ARN: `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:token-vault/${TokenVaultId}/apikeycredentialprovider/${Name}`
- CloudFormation: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::ApiKeyCredentialProvider`
- AWS Config: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::ApiKeyCredentialProvider`
- 8 operations, 3 threats, 2 mitigations

#### Browser

*COMPUTE_RESOURCE*

A browser is a managed, cloud-based web browser environment that AI agents use to interact with websites and web applications. Agents can navigate pages, fill out forms, click elements, capture screenshots, and extract content without running browser infrastructure themselves.

- IAM resource ARNs: `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:browser-custom/${BrowserId}`, `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:aws:browser/${BrowserId}`
- CloudFormation: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::BrowserCustom`, `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Browser`
- AWS Config: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::BrowserCustom`
- 7 operations, 6 threats, 6 mitigations

#### BrowserProfile

*DATA_STORE*

A browser profile in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser stores browser state, such as cookies and local storage, captured from a browser session. New sessions can start from that saved state, so they begin where an earlier session left off.

- IAM resource ARN: `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:browser-profile/${BrowserProfileId}`
- CloudFormation: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::BrowserProfile`
- 7 operations, 1 threats, 1 mitigations

#### CapacityProvider

*COMPUTE_RESOURCE*

A capacity provider defines the Amazon EC2 infrastructure that Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime uses for the Instances compute type. It specifies the operating system, allowed instance types, VPC placement, storage volumes, and the IAM roles used to operate the instances. A single capacity provider is reusable across multiple agent runtimes.

- IAM resource ARN: `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:capacity-provider/${CapacityProviderId}`
- CloudFormation: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::CapacityProvider`
- 9 operations, 14 threats, 10 mitigations

#### CodeInterpreter

*COMPUTE_RESOURCE*

A code interpreter gives AI agents a managed, sandboxed environment for writing, running, and debugging code. It helps agents perform precise calculations, data analysis, file processing, and visualization tasks that are difficult to solve through reasoning alone.

- IAM resource ARNs: `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:code-interpreter-custom/${CodeInterpreterId}`, `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:aws:code-interpreter/${CodeInterpreterId}`
- CloudFormation: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::CodeInterpreter`, `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::CodeInterpreterCustom`
- AWS Config: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::CodeInterpreterCustom`
- 7 operations, 8 threats, 7 mitigations

#### ConfigurationBundle

*CONFIGURATION*

A configuration bundle holds the dynamic settings an AgentCore agent reads at runtime, such as system prompts, model IDs, and tool descriptions. It separates agent behavior from agent code, so teams can adjust how an agent responds without redeploying it.

- IAM resource ARN: `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:configuration-bundle/${ConfigurationBundleId}`
- CloudFormation: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::ConfigurationBundle`, `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::ConfigurationBundleVersion`
- 7 operations, 5 threats, 2 mitigations

#### ConsentPortal

*IDENTITY*

A consent portal is an AWS-hosted web experience where end users grant an agent permission to access external services on their behalf. Users sign in through your organization's OpenID Connect identity provider, review the available service connections, and approve each one individually.

- IAM resource ARN: `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:consent-portal/${ConsentPortalId}`
- CloudFormation: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::ConsentPortal`
- 5 operations, 4 threats, 3 mitigations

#### Dataset

*DATA_STORE*

A dataset is a managed collection of test scenarios used to evaluate AI agents built with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Each scenario records the inputs sent to an agent and optional ground truth, such as expected responses, tool sequences, and assertions.

- IAM resource ARN: `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:dataset/${DatasetId}`
- CloudFormation: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Dataset`
- 7 operations, 3 threats, 2 mitigations

#### DatasetExample

*DATA_STORE*

A dataset example is a single evaluation scenario stored in an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore dataset. Each example describes a conversation used to test an agent, either as scripted user turns or as a simulated user persona with a goal.

- 4 operations, 0 threats, 0 mitigations

#### Evaluator

*AI_RESOURCE*

An evaluator defines how Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations scores the quality of an AI agent. It assesses agent behavior for a single tool call, a request-response trace, or a full conversation session.

- IAM resource ARN: `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:evaluator/${EvaluatorId}`
- CloudFormation: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Evaluator`
- AWS Config: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Evaluator`
- 8 operations, 5 threats, 2 mitigations

#### Gateway

*INTEGRATION*

An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway gives AI agents one managed endpoint for reaching tools, other agents, and large language models. It turns existing APIs, serverless functions, and remote tool servers into Model Context Protocol tools that agents can discover and call.

- IAM resource ARN: `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:gateway/${GatewayId}`
- CloudFormation: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Gateway`, `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::ResourcePolicy`
- AWS Config: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Gateway`
- 11 operations, 17 threats, 15 mitigations

#### GatewayRateLimit

*CONFIGURATION*

A gateway rate limit defines throttling rules for traffic that flows through an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway. It caps request rates, model token consumption, and concurrent connections for the tools, models, and agents behind the gateway.

- CloudFormation: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::GatewayRateLimit`
- 6 operations, 0 threats, 0 mitigations

#### GatewayRule

*CONFIGURATION*

A gateway rule tells an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway how to handle requests that match specific criteria. Each rule belongs to one gateway and has a priority, optional conditions, and one or two actions.

- CloudFormation: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::GatewayRule`
- 5 operations, 0 threats, 0 mitigations

#### GatewayTarget

*INTEGRATION*

A gateway target defines a backend that an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway connects to on behalf of AI agents. It can front tools such as AWS Lambda functions, REST APIs, and MCP servers, plus other agents and model providers. Each target pairs a backend endpoint with the outbound credentials the gateway uses, such as its service role, OAuth tokens, or stored API keys.

- CloudFormation: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::GatewayTarget`
- AWS Config: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::GatewayTarget`
- 6 operations, 5 threats, 5 mitigations

#### Harness

*AI_RESOURCE*

A harness is a managed agent definition in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. You declare the model, instructions, tools, skills, memory, and execution limits, and AgentCore runs the agent loop for you. Changing a model or adding a tool becomes a configuration change rather than a code rewrite.

- IAM resource ARN: `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:harness/${HarnessId}`
- CloudFormation: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Harness`, `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::HarnessVersion`
- 9 operations, 10 threats, 8 mitigations

#### HarnessEndpoint

*AI_RESOURCE*

A harness endpoint is a named, stable entry point for invoking a specific version of an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness. Callers target the endpoint by name, so the version behind it can change without changing how the agent is called.

- IAM resource ARN: `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:harness/${HarnessId}/harness-endpoint/${Name}`
- CloudFormation: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::HarnessEndpoint`
- 5 operations, 1 threats, 1 mitigations

#### Memory

*DATA_STORE*

An AgentCore memory gives AI agents a managed place to keep conversation history and learned context. It helps agents stay coherent within a conversation and personalize interactions across separate sessions.

- IAM resource ARN: `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:memory/${MemoryId}`
- CloudFormation: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Memory`
- AWS Config: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Memory`
- 8 operations, 7 threats, 5 mitigations

#### Oauth2CredentialProvider

*CRYPTOGRAPHIC_MATERIAL*

An OAuth2 credential provider holds the client credentials and endpoint settings for an external OAuth 2.0 authorization server. AgentCore Identity uses it to obtain access tokens so agents can call third-party services and internal APIs. Preconfigured settings cover popular services such as Google, GitHub, Slack, and Salesforce. A custom configuration works with other OAuth 2.0-compatible servers through discovery or manually entered endpoints.

- IAM resource ARN: `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:token-vault/${TokenVaultId}/oauth2credentialprovider/${Name}`
- CloudFormation: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::OAuth2CredentialProvider`
- AWS Config: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::OAuth2CredentialProvider`
- 8 operations, 7 threats, 5 mitigations

#### OnlineEvaluationConfig

*MONITORING*

An online evaluation configuration continuously assesses the quality of an AI agent running in production. It samples completed agent sessions from the agent's telemetry in Amazon CloudWatch Logs and scores them with selected evaluators. Evaluation runs asynchronously alongside live traffic and is designed not to add latency to user responses.

- IAM resource ARN: `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:online-evaluation-config/${OnlineEvaluationConfigId}`
- CloudFormation: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::OnlineEvaluationConfig`
- AWS Config: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::OnlineEvaluationConfig`
- 8 operations, 3 threats, 3 mitigations

#### PaymentConnector

*INTEGRATION*

A payment connector links your AgentCore payments configuration to an external wallet provider, such as Coinbase Developer Platform or Stripe with Privy. It lets agents sign payments for paid APIs, MCP servers, and web content through that provider's wallet infrastructure.

- CloudFormation: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::PaymentConnector`
- 6 operations, 0 threats, 0 mitigations

#### PaymentCredentialProvider

*CRYPTOGRAPHIC_MATERIAL*

A payment credential provider stores the credentials that AgentCore payments uses to work with an external wallet provider. Supported providers include Coinbase Developer Platform and Stripe with Privy. The provider keeps API keys, app secrets, wallet secrets, and authorization keys in AWS Secrets Manager rather than in agent code.

- IAM resource ARN: `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:token-vault/${TokenVaultId}/paymentcredentialprovider/${Name}`
- CloudFormation: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::PaymentCredentialProvider`
- 8 operations, 1 threats, 1 mitigations

#### PaymentManager

*RESOURCE_GROUPING*

A payment manager coordinates how your AI agents pay for APIs, MCP servers, and web content on behalf of end users. It serves as the configuration and authorization boundary for agent payment activity in an account and Region.

- IAM resource ARN: `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:payment-manager/${PaymentManagerId}`
- CloudFormation: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::PaymentManager`
- AWS Config: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::PaymentManager`
- 8 operations, 10 threats, 8 mitigations

#### Policy

*ACCESS_CONTROL*

A policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is an authorization rule that governs how AI agents use tools exposed through AgentCore Gateway. Each policy belongs to a policy engine and is written in Cedar or in Dogwood, a Cedar-compatible language.

- IAM resource ARN: `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:policy-engine/${PolicyEngineId}/policy/${PolicyId}`
- CloudFormation: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Policy`
- AWS Config: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Policy`
- 7 operations, 0 threats, 0 mitigations

#### PolicyEngine

*ACCESS_CONTROL*

A policy engine stores authorization policies that govern what AI agents can do with their tools. When attached to one or more gateways, it evaluates each agent tool call and returns an allow or deny decision before the tool runs.

- IAM resource ARN: `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:policy-engine/${PolicyEngineId}`
- CloudFormation: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::PolicyEngine`
- AWS Config: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::PolicyEngine`
- 15 operations, 5 threats, 2 mitigations

#### PolicyGeneration

*JOB_OR_WORKFLOW*

A policy generation converts plain-English authorization requirements into candidate policies for a Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore policy engine. It helps teams define which agent tool calls are allowed without first learning a formal policy language.

- IAM resource ARN: `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:policy-engine/${PolicyEngineId}/policy-generation/${PolicyGenerationId}`
- CloudFormation: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::PolicyGeneration`
- 6 operations, 0 threats, 0 mitigations

#### Registry

*RESOURCE_GROUPING*

A registry is a centralized catalog for organizing and discovering MCP servers, agents, agent skills, and custom resources across your organization. It helps teams find and reuse approved tools and agents instead of rebuilding them. It also gives administrators one place to govern which resources builders can discover.

- IAM resource ARN: `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:registry/${RegistryId}`
- 5 operations, 4 threats, 4 mitigations

#### RegistryRecord

*AI_RESOURCE*

A registry record describes one AI resource in an AWS Agent Registry catalog. The resource can be an MCP server with its tools, an Agent-to-Agent (A2A) agent, an agent skill, or a custom resource. Each record holds the resource's name, version, description, and protocol-specific descriptor content. This metadata helps people and AI agents find existing resources and understand how to use them.

- IAM resource ARN: `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:registry/${RegistryId}/record/${RecordId}`
- 7 operations, 1 threats, 1 mitigations

#### TokenVault

*CRYPTOGRAPHIC_MATERIAL*

The token vault is the managed credential store behind Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity. It holds OAuth 2.0 access and refresh tokens, OAuth client credentials, and API keys that agents use to reach external tools and services. Each account uses a default vault in each AWS Region.

- IAM resource ARN: `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:token-vault/${TokenVaultId}`
- CloudFormation: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::TokenVault`
- AWS Config: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::TokenVault`
- 5 operations, 3 threats, 2 mitigations

#### WorkloadIdentity

*IDENTITY*

A workload identity gives an AI agent or automated workload its own stable, verifiable identity within an AWS account and Region. Agents use it to authenticate as themselves instead of impersonating users, wherever the agent runs.

- IAM resource ARN: `arn:${Partition}:bedrock-agentcore:${Region}:${Account}:workload-identity-directory/${DirectoryId}/workload-identity/${WorkloadIdentityName}`

- AWS Config: `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::WorkloadIdentity`
